item.title: Who We Are
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
St. Columba Parish is a Roman Catholic community of the Archdiocese of Toronto, rooted at the corner of Columba Avenue and Pape in East York. About 1,200 households call this their parish home. Some have been here since the church was dedicated in 1961; others arrived last month. Whether you are a lifelong Catholic, someone returning after years away, or simply curious, this page will tell you who we are and how to find your place among us.

A welcome from our pastor

Dear friends,

Thank you for visiting St. Columba, whether in person or through this website. A parish is not a building or a schedule of services. It is a family of people who gather around the altar every week, carry one another through sickness and loss, celebrate births and weddings together, and try, in an ordinary Toronto neighbourhood, to live as Jesus asked us to.

You will hear Mass here in English, Spanish, Tagalog and Italian, and you will meet families from Portugal, Sri Lanka, Nigeria, Ireland and dozens of other places. What unites us is far greater than what distinguishes us. If you are new, please introduce yourself after Mass. I would very much like to meet you.

In Christ,
Rev. Daniel Moreau
Pastor

The parish at a glance

1954 year founded
1,200 registered families
6 language communities
30+ ministries and groups

We celebrate seven Masses every weekend and one every weekday, hear confessions twice a week, and keep the church open for Adoration on Thursday mornings. The parish hall seats 220 people and hosts everything from First Communion breakfasts to the Knights' pasta dinner. See the full Mass and confession schedule or browse the ministry directory.

Our mission

St. Columba Parish exists to worship God, to form missionary disciples, and to serve our neighbours in East York with the love of Christ. We do this by celebrating the sacraments well, teaching the faith at every age, welcoming every person who walks through our doors, and sharing what we have with those who have less.

In practice, that mission takes the shape of a Sunday choir that has sung together for thirty years, a St. Vincent de Paul conference that visits about forty households a month, a youth group that fills the hall on Friday nights, and a catechetical program that prepares roughly ninety children a year for First Communion and Confirmation. Our 2025–2028 pastoral plan sets out where we hope to be in three years.

Our patron

Columba (521–597) was an Irish monk who founded the monastery of Iona and brought the Gospel to Scotland. The Irish families who built this parish chose him as a patron for a community of immigrants: a saint who left home to carry the faith somewhere new.

— St. Columba, pray for us. Feast day June 9

Our neighbourhood

East York was its own borough until amalgamation in 1998, and it still feels like a small town inside the city: brick semis, corner bakeries, the Danforth a short walk south. The parish sits a few blocks from Pape Station, with the parking lot behind the hall and a TTC stop at the door.

Our boundaries run roughly from the Don Valley east to Coxwell Avenue and from the Danforth north to O'Connor Drive, but you are welcome here wherever you live. Many parishioners drive in from Scarborough, Leaside and downtown because their family has always come, or because they found a community here.

Two Toronto Catholic District School Board schools sit within the parish, and we share a chaplaincy relationship with both. See our parish school page.

Find us

St. Columba Parish, 1240 Columba Avenue, Toronto, ON M4K 2R6
Office Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM–4:00 PM (closed 12–1) · 416-555-0142 · office@stcolumbatoronto.ca
Accessible entrance on the east side, elevator to the hall, hearing loop in the church. Details on our accessibility page.

Where to go next

If this is your first visit, start with our guide for newcomers. If you already know your way around, check the Mass schedule or find a group to join. Questions of any kind are welcome at the parish office, or ask any usher on Sunday.

item.title: Accessibility
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Everyone belongs at Mass. St. Columba Parish is committed to providing its services in a way that respects the dignity and independence of people with disabilities, and to meeting the requirements of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA) and the standards made under it. Our building dates from 1954, and we have been steadily adapting it since; the hearing loop, elevator and accessible washroom were added in 2019 through a parish campaign and a grant from the Archdiocese. Where a barrier remains, we will do our best to work around it with you.

Getting into the church and hall

  • Accessible entrance on the east side of the church (facing the parking lot), with a level path from the sidewalk, an automatic door opener and no steps. The main front doors have six steps and a handrail.
  • Elevator just inside the east entrance serving the church level, the lower-level parish hall and the washrooms.
  • Accessible washroom on the lower level beside the elevator, with an adult change bench and an emergency call button; a second accessible washroom is off the church vestibule.
  • Accessible parking: four designated spaces beside the east entrance. On Sundays the first row of the lot is reserved for people with mobility needs; ushers will direct you.
  • Drop-off: the east-side driveway loop allows drivers to stop at the door.

Inside the church

  • Pew cut-outs for wheelchairs and scooters at the front and back of the centre aisle and on both side aisles, so you can sit with your family rather than apart from them.
  • Hearing loop covering the whole nave. Switch your hearing aid or cochlear implant to the "T" setting. Loop receivers with headphones are available from the ushers for anyone without a T-coil.
  • Large-print missals and hymn sheets in the rack at each entrance, and large-print copies of the bulletin at the office.
  • Lighting on the sanctuary and ambo was upgraded in 2023 to reduce glare; the readings are also projected on the screens at the 11:00 AM Mass.
  • Seating with arms in the last three rows on each side, and a small number of chairs with higher seats at the back for anyone who finds pews difficult.
  • Service animals are welcome everywhere in the church and hall.

Taking part in Mass

Holy Communion is brought to anyone who cannot come forward. Simply stay in your pew and raise a hand, or let an usher know before Mass; a minister will come to you. Gluten-free (low-gluten) hosts are available; tell the priest or an usher before Mass and receive from the priest's line. The Sunday 11:00 AM Mass is livestreamed and archived for those who cannot attend in person. Confession is available in the reconciliation room, which is on the level of the church and large enough for a wheelchair, as well as in the traditional confessional.

If you or a family member has a disability that affects sacramental preparation, for example a child on the autism spectrum preparing for First Communion, please speak with Sr. Agnes (ext. 25). We have adapted materials and experience, and no one is excluded from the sacraments because of a disability.

Parish hall

The hall is reached by the elevator or the interior stairs, has a level floor, an accessible washroom, wide doors and an accessible route to the stage by ramp. Tables are set at wheelchair height on request. See Hall Rentals if you are planning an event.

Website accessibility

This website is designed to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA, the standard Ontario requires of public-facing websites. In practice that means:

  • All text can be resized to 200 per cent without losing content, and the site works at phone width.
  • Every image has a text description, and decorative images are hidden from screen readers.
  • All pages can be navigated by keyboard alone, with a visible focus indicator and a "skip to content" link.
  • Colour contrast meets the AA minimum, and colour is never the only way information is conveyed.
  • Videos on the livestream page carry captions where the source provides them.
  • Bulletins are posted as PDFs; if you need a bulletin in another format, the office will email you the text.

We test the site with a screen reader and keyboard each time it is redesigned, but we know issues can slip through. If you find a page that does not work for you, please tell us using the feedback process below and we will fix it as quickly as we can.

Feedback and requests

  1. Tell us

    Call 416-555-0142 ext. 21, email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "Accessibility" in the subject line, use the contact form, or speak to any usher or staff member. We accept feedback in any format, including in person or by mail.

  2. We acknowledge it

    You will hear back within five business days, in the format you prefer.

  3. We act

    Small fixes, such as a website issue or a missing large-print missal, are handled right away. Larger requests go to the pastor and the Finance Council; we will tell you what we can do and when.

Documents such as this policy, our privacy policy and registration forms are available on request in large print or by email. Our accessibility contact is Teresa Alvarez, Office Manager. For information about the AODA and your rights under it, see ontario.ca/accessibility.

Frequently asked

Can someone meet me at the door?

Yes. Call the office ahead of time or ask a greeter, and an usher will meet you at the east entrance and help you to a seat.

Is there a quiet space if my child becomes overwhelmed?

The vestibule cry room at the back of the church has a window and speaker so you can still follow Mass. It is open at every Mass.

Do you offer Mass in sign language?

Not at St. Columba at present. The Archdiocese supports a Deaf ministry with interpreted Masses at a downtown parish; the office can give you the details.

item.title: Eucharistic Adoration
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Adoration is simply keeping company with Jesus, present in the Eucharist, outside of Mass. The Blessed Sacrament is placed in the monstrance on the altar, the church is quiet, and you stay as long as you can. People bring a Bible or a rosary; many bring nothing at all.

Weekly

  • Exposition after the 8:30 MassThu
  • Silent adoration9:00 – 11:45
  • Benediction11:45 AM

First Friday

  • Exposition7:00 PM
  • Confessions available7:00 – 7:45
  • Benediction7:50 PM

Also

  • Youth adoration nightmonthly, see events
  • Holy Thursdayuntil midnight
  • Forty HoursLent

Sign up for an hour

The Blessed Sacrament is never left alone, so we ask parishioners to commit to a regular half-hour or hour on Thursday mornings. About thirty adorers currently share the morning; we always need a few more, especially between 10:00 and 11:00. To join, email adorers@stcolumbatoronto.ca or sign the sheet at the back of the church. If you cannot make your hour, text the coordinator, Rosa Fernandes, and she will find a substitute.

What to do in adoration

  • Genuflect on both knees when you arrive and leave, if you are able.
  • Sit or kneel; there is no programme and no one is watching.
  • Read the day's Gospel slowly, pray the rosary, or just be still.
  • Speak to the Lord as you would to a friend — about what is really on your mind.
  • Keep silence in the church; the narthex is the place for conversation.

Prayers for adoration

Prayer on arriving

Lord Jesus, I believe you are truly here. I have come to be with you. Quiet my heart, open my ears, and let me rest in your presence. Amen.

The Divine Praises (prayed at Benediction)

Blessed be God. Blessed be his holy Name. Blessed be Jesus Christ, true God and true Man. Blessed be the Name of Jesus. Blessed be his most Sacred Heart. Blessed be his most Precious Blood. Blessed be Jesus in the most Holy Sacrament of the Altar. Blessed be the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Blessed be the great Mother of God, Mary most holy. Blessed be her holy and Immaculate Conception. Blessed be her glorious Assumption. Blessed be the name of Mary, Virgin and Mother. Blessed be St. Joseph, her most chaste spouse. Blessed be God in his angels and in his saints.

Is adoration suitable for children?

Yes — for ten or fifteen minutes. Sit near the back so you can slip out. The children's liturgy team runs a short guided adoration for families on the first Thursday of each month at 9:15 AM.

item.title: Altar Servers
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Altar servers carry the cross and candles, hold the book, present the bread and wine, ring the bells and — most importantly — show the congregation how to pray by their attention. Sixty-five servers, aged eight to seventy-two, serve at St. Columba. Girls and boys serve equally; a growing number of adults serve at weekday Masses and funerals.

Who

  • ChildrenGrade 3+, after First Communion
  • Teenssenior servers & trainers
  • Adultsweekday Masses, funerals

Training

  • Three Saturday sessions10 AM
  • OfferedOct & Feb
  • Commissioning at Mass

Serving

  • Monthly rota2–3 Masses
  • Weddings & funeralssign-up, $10 stipend
  • Arrive20 min before

What we ask

  • Serve the Masses you are scheduled for, or find a swap and tell the coordinator.
  • Arrive twenty minutes early; vest in the sacristy; phones stay in the sacristy.
  • Dress: dark trousers or skirt, dark shoes, no sports jerseys under the alb.
  • Reverence in the sanctuary — no whispering, no waving to parents (a smile is fine).
  • Keep learning: senior servers train the juniors and take the harder roles (thurifer, master of ceremonies) at feasts.

The year

Training sessions in October and February cover the parts of the Mass, the vessels and their names, processions and the roles of crossbearer, candle-bearers, book-bearer and thurifer. New servers are commissioned at the 11:00 AM Mass and receive a St. Columba server's medal. The Holy Week liturgies are the highlight of the year and the senior servers' privilege. In June the whole group goes to Canada's Wonderland, paid for by the Knights of Columbus; there is a pizza night at Christmas, and servers who have given five years receive the parish's silver cross.

For parents

How much time is it?

Two or three Masses a month, chosen from the Mass your family already attends. Schedules come out two months ahead by email and are posted in the sacristy.

My child is nervous.

Everyone starts as a candle-bearer beside a senior server, with nothing to say and little to carry. Confidence comes within a month.

Is it safe?

All adult servers, trainers and sacristans are screened; children are never alone with an adult in the sacristy, which has a glass door; and the sacristan is present at every vesting. Parents are welcome in the sacristy at any time.

Do servers get paid for weddings and funerals?

Families customarily give a small stipend ($10–20) which servers may keep or, as many do, put in the poor box.

Coordinator: Deacon Paul Ferreira, ext. 24 · Senior server captain: Olivia Chen · servers@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

item.title: Anointing of the Sick
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
When someone we love is seriously ill, we want to do something. The Church gives us something to do: call the priest. In the Anointing of the Sick, a priest lays his hands on the person, anoints their forehead and hands with blessed oil, and prays that the Lord "who frees you from sin save you and raise you up." It is a sacrament of healing and peace, not a farewell. Please do not wait until the last hours; the anointing does its best work when the person can take part in it, and it can be received more than once.

Who can receive it

Any baptized Catholic who has reached the age of reason and whose health is seriously impaired by illness or age. In practice that includes:

  • anyone about to undergo surgery under general anaesthetic, or a serious procedure;
  • anyone diagnosed with a serious or chronic illness, including cancer, heart disease, dementia and serious mental illness;
  • the elderly who are noticeably weakened, even without a specific diagnosis;
  • children old enough to understand what is happening, when seriously ill;
  • anyone whose condition worsens after a previous anointing, or who has recovered and become ill again.

A person who is unconscious or unable to respond can still be anointed if they would have asked for it. The sacrament is not celebrated for someone who has already died; in that case the priest comes to pray with the family and commend the person to God, which is itself a great comfort.

When and how to call

To request an anointing

Office hours (Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM–4:00 PM): phone 416-555-0142 and ask for a priest. If both priests are out, the office will reach one and call you back within the hour.

After hours and weekends, in an emergency: phone 416-555-0142 and press extension 9. This rings the on-call priest directly, day or night. Please use it only for someone who is in danger of death or being taken to hospital urgently.

When you call, tell us the person's name, where they are (home, hospital and ward, or care home and room), how urgent it is, and a phone number for someone who will be with them. If the person can no longer speak, tell us whether they were a practising Catholic and whether they would want the sacrament. The priest comes to the home, to any hospital in the city, or to a long-term care residence. Hospitals in Toronto also have Catholic chaplains on call; ask the nurse to page the chaplain if a parish priest cannot reach you in time. See hospital chaplaincies for details.

What happens during the anointing

  1. Greeting and preparation

    The priest greets the sick person and the family, sprinkles the room with holy water and invites everyone to pray. If the person wishes to go to confession, family step out for a few minutes.

  2. Word of God

    A short Gospel passage is read, often the healing of the paralytic or the story of Bartimaeus, followed by prayers for the sick person, their carers and their doctors.

  3. Laying on of hands

    In silence, the priest lays his hands on the person's head, as Jesus did with the sick.

  4. Anointing

    He anoints the forehead and the palms of the hands with the Oil of the Sick, blessed by the Archbishop each Holy Week, and prays: "Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit. May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up."

  5. Communion and blessing

    If the person can receive, the priest gives Holy Communion. For someone close to death, this Communion is called viaticum, "food for the journey," and is the sacrament the Church most wants a dying Christian to receive. The rite ends with a blessing for everyone in the room.

The whole rite takes fifteen to twenty minutes. Family and friends of any faith are welcome to stay and pray; it helps to have a small table with a cloth, a candle and a glass of water ready if the priest is coming to a home.

Communal anointing Mass

Twice a year, on the Saturday nearest 11 February (World Day of the Sick) and on a Saturday in October, we celebrate an Anointing Mass at 11:00 AM for anyone who is elderly, chronically ill or facing surgery. The church is arranged so that nobody has to walk far, the Knights of Columbus provide transport from home for those who need it, and lunch follows in the hall. Please phone the office to book a ride. Family members do not receive the anointing but are warmly welcome to come.

Communion to the homebound

If you or a family member cannot come to Mass because of illness, age or disability, one of our Lay Pastoral Visitors will bring Holy Communion to you at home, usually weekly on Sunday afternoon or a weekday of your choosing. The visitors are trained and commissioned parishioners, screened under the Archdiocese's Safe Environment policy, and they bring the Sunday bulletin and a friendly face as well as the Eucharist. A priest visits each homebound parishioner every few months for confession and anointing. To arrange visits, phone the office or email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca; see also seniors' ministry.

Frequently asked questions

Is this the same as "Last Rites"?

"Last Rites" is an older name for the prayers offered to a dying person, which include confession, anointing and viaticum. Since the Second Vatican Council the Church has been clear that anointing is for the seriously ill, not only the dying. Asking for it early is a sign of faith, not of giving up.

My mother is in a care home outside the parish. Will you come?

Yes, anywhere in the city. If she is far from us, we may also ask the nearest parish to add her to their regular visits, so she is seen more often.

Can a deacon or a lay visitor anoint?

Only a priest can anoint. Deacons and Lay Pastoral Visitors bring Communion, pray with the sick and let the priest know when an anointing is needed.

Is there a fee?

No. There is never a charge for the sacraments of the sick or for visiting the dying.

What should we do when someone dies?

Call the parish as soon as you are able, and then a funeral home. Our funerals page walks you through the next days gently and in order.

Questions? Phone the parish office at 416-555-0142, or in an emergency after hours press extension 9. You are never troubling us; this is what we are here for.

Ask for prayers

item.title: Archdiocese of Toronto
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
A parish is never an island. St. Columba belongs to the Archdiocese of Toronto, the family of Catholic parishes, schools, hospitals, cemeteries and charities that stretches from Lake Ontario north to Georgian Bay and from Oshawa west to Mississauga. The Archdiocese is led by the Archbishop of Toronto, assisted by auxiliary bishops, and it serves close to two million Catholics who worship in more than three dozen languages every Sunday. Our parish shares in that wider mission, and the offices of the Archdiocese in turn support the work we do here in East York.

What the Archdiocese is

In the Catholic Church, a diocese is a territory entrusted to a bishop, who is the chief teacher, shepherd and priest of the local Church. Because Toronto is a metropolitan see, its bishop holds the title of Archbishop. The Archbishop of Toronto appoints and assigns priests, oversees the seminary, approves parish boundaries and building projects, and is responsible for the teaching of the faith across the whole region. The chancery (the Catholic Pastoral Centre downtown) houses the offices that coordinate everything from marriage tribunals and Catholic education to refugee sponsorship and youth ministry.

The cathedral of the Archdiocese is St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica on Bond Street. Every parish is invited to the Chrism Mass held there in Holy Week, when the Archbishop blesses the holy oils that we use at baptisms, confirmations, ordinations and anointings throughout the year.

How our parish relates to the Archdiocese

Fr. Moreau and Fr. Nguyen are priests of the Archdiocese, assigned to St. Columba by the Archbishop. Deacon Ferreira was ordained by the Archbishop for service in this region. Our parish follows archdiocesan policy on finances, volunteer screening, sacramental records and safe environment, and we file an annual financial report with the chancery. In practical terms, this means a few things for you as a parishioner:

  • Your donations are receipted under our own charitable registration, but online giving runs through the secure archdiocesan portal.
  • Sacramental records (baptisms, confirmations, marriages) are kept here and copied to the archdiocesan archive, so a certificate can be found even decades later.
  • Marriage annulment cases, permissions for mixed marriages and dispensations are handled by the archdiocesan Marriage Tribunal and Chancery, with our clergy helping you prepare the paperwork.
  • Our parish pays an annual assessment to the Archdiocese that funds the seminary, retired priests, chaplaincies and central services.

Good to know

St. Columba is part of the Central Region of the Archdiocese, and belongs to a deanery of neighbouring East York and Riverdale parishes whose pastors meet monthly. If you move within the Archdiocese, your sacramental records stay searchable, and you can simply register at your new parish.

Services

Archdiocesan offices and services

Many of the ministries that touch parish life are run centrally. These are the ones parishioners ask about most often.

Pastoral care

Chaplaincies

Catholic chaplains serve Toronto's hospitals, universities, prisons and long-term-care homes. Learn how to request a chaplain for a loved one.

Chaplaincies

ORAT

Refugee Sponsorship

The Office for Refugees helps parishes like ours welcome families fleeing persecution. Our sponsorship committee is always looking for help.

Refugee sponsorship

Office of Vocations

Vocations

Discerning priesthood, the permanent diaconate or consecrated life? The Office of Vocations and our parish can walk with you.

Vocations

External

Catholic Cemeteries & Funeral Services

The Archdiocese operates Catholic cemeteries across the region, including Mount Hope and Holy Cross, and offers pre-planning consultations.

catholic-cemeteries.ca

External

ShareLife

The annual archdiocesan appeal funds more than 40 agencies serving families, seniors, newcomers and people with disabilities. Our parish goal is set each spring.

sharelife.org

External

Formation for Discipleship

Courses, retreats and resources for adults who want to grow in faith and lead in their parish, offered by the Archdiocese.

archtoronto.org

Policy

Safe Environment

The Strengthening the Caring Community policy sets out how every parish protects children and vulnerable adults, and how concerns are reported.

Safe environment

Frequently asked

Can I attend Mass at any parish in the Archdiocese?

Yes. You may worship anywhere, and your Sunday obligation is fulfilled at any Catholic Mass. Registering with one parish simply lets us serve you well with envelopes, sacramental preparation and records.

Where do I get a copy of a baptism certificate from another Toronto parish?

Contact the parish where the baptism took place. If that church has closed or merged, the Archdiocesan Archives holds its registers; our office can tell you who to call.

How does the Archbishop visit parishes?

The Archbishop or an auxiliary bishop comes to St. Columba for Confirmation each spring and for anniversaries and special occasions. Pastoral visits are announced in the bulletin well ahead of time.

Questions about anything on this page? Contact Ann Marie O'Connor at the parish office, 416-555-0142 ext. 20, or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca, and we will point you to the right archdiocesan office.

Visit archtoronto.org

item.title: Baptism
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Baptism is the door to everything else: through water and the Holy Spirit a child becomes a Christian and a member of the Church. We baptize children of any age; for children over seven and for adults, see Becoming Catholic.

When

  • Baptisms2nd & 4th Sundays2:30 PM
  • Within Sunday Massby arrangement11:00 AM
  • Preparation classlast Saturday of the month2:00 PM

Bring

  • Child's birth certificate
  • Godparents' names & parish
  • Registration form
  • White garment & candleor buy at the office

Cost

  • No fee
  • Offering welcomecustomary $50–100
  • CertificateFree

Step by step

  1. Register with the parish

    Baptisms are celebrated for families who live in the parish or worship here. If you are not yet registered, register online — it takes five minutes. Families from another parish need a letter of permission from their own pastor.

  2. Submit the baptism form

    Download the registration form (PDF) or collect it from the office. Return it with a copy of the birth certificate at least four weeks before the date you would like.

  3. Attend the preparation evening

    One session for parents and godparents, on the last Saturday of the month at 2:00 PM in the hall, about ninety minutes, children welcome. It explains the rite and what you are promising. Godparents who live far away may attend a class at their own parish and send the certificate.

  4. Choose the date

    Baptisms take place on the second and fourth Sundays at 2:30 PM, usually three or four children together. A baptism within the 11:00 AM Mass — where the whole community welcomes your child — can be arranged for registered families.

  5. The day

    Arrive twenty minutes early. The rite takes about forty-five minutes. Photographs are welcome; a video from the side aisle is fine. Please ask guests to keep phones silent.

Choosing godparents

A godparent promises to help the parents raise the child in the faith, so the Church asks that at least one godparent be a practising Catholic, at least 16, who has been confirmed and, if married, married in the Church. A baptized Christian of another denomination may stand as a "Christian witness" alongside a Catholic godparent. One godparent is enough; two — a godmother and a godfather — is customary. Godparents will need a letter of good standing from their own parish.

Questions

One of us is not Catholic. Can our child be baptized?

Yes. What matters is that there is a reasonable hope the child will be raised Catholic. Both parents are welcome at the preparation evening and take a full part in the rite.

We are not married, or not married in the Church.

Your child is welcome for baptism. If you would like to talk about your own situation — including having a civil marriage blessed — Fr. Moreau would be glad to; there is no pressure.

Our child is older than two.

Children up to about age six are baptized as infants with a little more explanation for them. Children seven and older prepare with a short children's program (RCIC) so that they understand and choose what is happening.

Can we baptize in an emergency?

item.title: Becoming Catholic (OCIA)
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Every year a dozen or so adults are baptized, received into the Church or confirmed at St. Columba's Easter Vigil. Some married a Catholic and grew curious; some were baptized as babies and never went further; some walked in off Pape Avenue one Sunday and kept coming back. The Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, or OCIA (formerly RCIA), is the path the Church offers. It is unhurried, free, and begins with a conversation.

Who OCIA is for

Never baptized

Adults seeking baptism

If you have never been baptized in any Christian church, OCIA prepares you to receive Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion together at the Easter Vigil. You are called a catechumen once you formally enter the process.

Baptized in another church

Christians becoming Catholic

If you were baptized Anglican, United, Baptist, Orthodox or in another Christian tradition, the Church recognizes your baptism. You prepare to make a profession of faith and receive Confirmation and Communion. You are called a candidate.

Baptized Catholic

Catholics completing their sacraments

If you were baptized Catholic but never made your First Communion or were never confirmed, OCIA is for you too. Many in the group each year are in exactly this situation, often in their twenties, thirties or forties.

The stages

The process follows four stages with a liturgical rite marking the passage from each to the next. Most people move through it in one year, but nobody is held to a calendar; if you need longer, you take longer.

  1. Inquiry (September to November)

    Come and ask questions. The first weeks are open conversations about God, Jesus, prayer and the Church. Nothing is signed; if this is not for you, you leave with our thanks.

  2. Catechumenate (December to February)

    At the Rite of Acceptance, celebrated at a Sunday Mass in late November, you are welcomed by the parish and begin structured teaching on the Creed, the sacraments, the moral life and prayer. You attend Sunday Mass and are dismissed after the homily to reflect on the readings with your catechist.

  3. Purification and enlightenment (Lent)

    On the first Sunday of Lent, the Archbishop of Toronto or his delegate celebrates the Rite of Election at the cathedral for all the catechumens of the Archdiocese, and your name is written in the Book of the Elect. Lent is a retreat: fewer lessons, more prayer, three "scrutinies" at Sunday Mass, and a day of reflection in March.

  4. Sacraments at the Easter Vigil, then mystagogy

    On Holy Saturday night you are baptized and confirmed and receive Communion for the first time, in a church full of candles and parishioners who have been praying for you. The weeks of Easter that follow, called mystagogy, are for unpacking what happened and finding your place in the parish.

When and where we meet

Tuesdays, 7:00–8:30 PM, in the rectory meeting room, from the second Tuesday of September until the Easter Vigil. Sessions are led by Sr. Agnes Ibeh with a team of four parish catechists and Fr. Nguyen, who joins most weeks. Coffee and tea are on; some people come straight from work. There are no sessions during Christmas week or March Break. Reading material is provided, and there is no charge of any kind.

You may join at any point during the inquiry stage. If you find us in February, come anyway; we will talk about the best way forward for you.

Sponsors

Every catechumen and candidate has a sponsor: a practising Catholic who walks beside you, sits with you at Mass, answers the questions you are embarrassed to ask in the group, and stands with you at the Vigil. A spouse cannot serve as a sponsor for baptism, but a friend or in-law can. If you do not know anyone, the parish will match you with a trained sponsor from the OCIA team.

Children and teenagers

OCIC: initiation for children of school age

Children aged seven to sixteen who have not been baptized, or who were baptized but have missed First Communion or Confirmation, are prepared through a parallel process on Sunday mornings during the school year, in age-appropriate groups. Parents attend several sessions with them. Younger children are baptized through the ordinary infant baptism preparation. Contact Sr. Agnes to discuss which path fits your child.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to decide to become Catholic before I start?

No. The inquiry stage exists precisely so that you can look before you commit. Some people take two years; some decide the Catholic Church is not for them, and part as friends.

I was married outside the Church, or I am divorced. Is that a problem?

It is a common situation and usually workable, but it needs to be looked at early. Please mention it in your first conversation with Sr. Agnes or Fr. Nguyen so that any steps, such as having a marriage blessed or seeking an annulment, can start in good time.

Do I need to attend Mass during OCIA?

Yes, from the Rite of Acceptance onward. Sunday Mass is where the parish meets Christ, and it is the best classroom there is. Most people find the 11:00 AM Mass works well because the group is dismissed together after the homily.

What documents will I need?

If you were baptized in another church, a copy of your baptismal certificate or a letter from that church. If you are unbaptized, nothing. Catholics completing their sacraments need a recent baptismal certificate from the parish of baptism; we can help you request it.

Take the first step

Contact Sr. Agnes Ibeh, SSND, Pastoral Associate and Catechetical Coordinator, at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca or 416-555-0142 ext. 25. She will suggest a half-hour meeting, in person or by phone, to hear your story. That conversation commits you to nothing.

item.title: Beliefs & Teachings
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
This page is not a textbook. It is a map: the main things the Catholic Church believes, each in a paragraph, with a pointer to where the full teaching can be read. Where we say "the Church teaches," the authoritative source is the Catechism of the Catholic Church, which is free to read online.

The Creed

Every Sunday the whole congregation stands and says the Nicene Creed, a summary of the faith agreed by the bishops of the world in the fourth century. Its main affirmations are these:

  • One God in three Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, who created everything that exists.
  • Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who took on human flesh through the Virgin Mary, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, died and was buried, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven.
  • The Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets and gives life to the Church.
  • The Church, which is one, holy, catholic (meaning universal) and apostolic (founded on the apostles and led by their successors, the bishops in union with the Pope).
  • One baptism for the forgiveness of sins.
  • The resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.

The shorter Apostles' Creed, used in the Rosary and at baptisms, is on our prayers page.

The seven sacraments

A sacrament is a visible sign, instituted by Christ, through which God gives grace. There are seven. Baptism makes us children of God and members of the Church. Confirmation strengthens us with the Holy Spirit. The Eucharist feeds us with the Body and Blood of Christ. Reconciliation (confession) forgives sins committed after baptism. Anointing of the Sick brings Christ's healing to the seriously ill. Marriage unites a man and a woman in a lifelong covenant. Holy Orders ordains deacons, priests and bishops to serve the Church.

Each sacrament, and how to receive it here, is explained on our sacraments pages.

The Mass and the Eucharist

The Mass is the centre of Catholic life. In it, the Church does what Jesus commanded at the Last Supper: takes bread and wine, gives thanks, and shares them in his memory. Catholics believe that at the words of consecration the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ, while keeping the appearance of bread and wine; the Church's word for this is transubstantiation. That is why we kneel, why we keep the consecrated Hosts in the tabernacle with a lamp burning beside it, and why we set aside Thursday mornings for Adoration. Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday and holy day. Our full schedule is on Mass times.

Mary and the saints

Catholics do not worship Mary or the saints; worship belongs to God alone. We honour them and ask for their prayers, as you might ask a friend to pray for you. Mary holds a unique place as the Mother of Jesus. The Church teaches that she was conceived without sin (the Immaculate Conception), remained a virgin, and at the end of her life was taken body and soul into heaven (the Assumption). The saints are men and women whom the Church has recognized as being with God, and whose lives show us that holiness is possible in every century and every walk of life. Our parish honours St. Columba, and our language communities keep the feasts of Our Lady of Fátima, San Lorenzo Ruiz and Our Lady of Guadalupe. See devotions.

Catholic social teaching

Faith that does not change how we treat other people is not the faith of the Gospel. Over the past 130 years the popes have set out principles for a just society, which the Church calls its social teaching:

  • The dignity of the human person — every life is sacred, from conception to natural death, regardless of ability, status or usefulness.
  • The common good — society is judged by whether it lets everyone flourish, not only the fortunate.
  • Solidarity — we are one human family, responsible for one another across borders and generations.
  • Subsidiarity — decisions should be made at the most local level that can make them well.
  • A preferential option for the poor — the needs of the poor and vulnerable come first.
  • The dignity of work — work serves people, not the other way round; workers have a right to fair wages and to organize.
  • Care for creation — the earth is a gift to be stewarded, not a resource to be used up.

At St. Columba this teaching takes shape in the St. Vincent de Paul conference, our refugee sponsorship group, the annual ShareLife appeal, and the work of Development and Peace, the Canadian Church's international development agency. See outreach.

Recommended resources

Catechism of the Catholic Church

The complete, official summary of Catholic teaching: Part One for beliefs, Two for the sacraments, Three for the moral life, Four for prayer.

Read online at vatican.va

FORMED

Video series, audio talks, films and children's programs on the faith. St. Columba has a parish subscription, so parishioners can sign up free using the parish name and postal code.

formed.org

Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops

Statements, pastoral letters and resources from the bishops of Canada, including materials on reconciliation with Indigenous peoples and Catholic responses to public questions.

cccb.ca

Archdiocese of Toronto

Our own diocese: news, the Cardinal's letters, Formation for Discipleship courses for adults, and directories of parishes and services.

archtoronto.org

Parishioners also recommend the books and videos of Bishop Robert Barron's Word on Fire ministry, several of which are in the parish lending library in the hall foyer.

Questions about any of this are welcome. Email Sr. Agnes Ibeh at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca, or, if you are ready for something more structured, read about Becoming Catholic and faith formation for adults.

item.title: Bereavement Ministry
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
In the weeks after a funeral, people rally. In the months after, the house goes quiet. Our bereavement ministry — twelve trained volunteers, most of whom have walked this road themselves — is there for the quiet months. Everything below is free and open to anyone, parishioner or not, whether or not the funeral was here.

Group

Grief support group

Eight Tuesday evenings, 7:00–8:30 PM, twice a year (starting the last week of September and the first week of March). Eight to twelve people, two facilitators, a simple structure: a theme each week — shock, anger, guilt, loneliness, faith, the "firsts", hope — and time to talk or just listen. Confidential. Most people join three to twelve months after a death.

One-to-one

Bereavement companions

A trained volunteer who visits or phones weekly for as long as it helps — often a year. Companions are matched thoughtfully (a widow with a widow, a bereaved parent with a bereaved parent) and are not counsellors; they are people who will let you tell the story again.

Liturgy

Remembering

The All Souls' Day Mass on November 2 at 7:00 PM, when every family we have buried in the past year is invited by name and a candle is lit for each; the parish Book of the Dead in the narthex; anniversary Mass intentions; and a Blue Christmas prayer service in mid-December for those for whom the season is hard.

What grief is like

It is not a set of stages you pass through in order. It is more like weather: some days clear, some days you cannot get out of bed, and no way to predict which. Faith does not remove grief — Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb — but it gives it a horizon. You are allowed to be angry with God; he can take it. You are allowed to laugh again; it is not a betrayal. You do not have to be "over it" by any date. And you do not have to do it alone.

Also here for you

  • Funeral receptions in the hall, prepared by the CWL, so the family can be with their guests.
  • Practical help from the St. Vincent de Paul conference if a death has left a household in difficulty.
  • Prayer: the prayer chain prays for the bereaved by name; the Legion of Mary visits after a funeral.
  • Children and teens: the youth minister and Sr. Agnes can meet a grieving child or refer to specialized children's grief programs in Toronto.
  • Pregnancy and infant loss: a memorial Mass each October 15, and companions who have experienced this loss.
  • Suicide loss: a companion trained in suicide bereavement, and a referral to a survivors' group. The Church prays for those who die by suicide with the same hope as for anyone.

If you are in crisis

If grief has become despair and you are thinking of harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8 (Canada's suicide crisis helpline, 24 hours) or go to the nearest emergency department. Then call us; we will be there.

Questions

How do I join the group?

Email or phone the coordinator; a facilitator will have a short conversation with you first so that the group is a good fit. Sessions start in late September and early March.

The death was years ago. Is it too late?

No. Grief that was never given room often surfaces years later. Come.

Can I become a companion?

Volunteers who are at least two years from their own loss complete a six-session archdiocesan training and high-risk screening, and meet monthly for supervision.

Coordinator: Patricia Nolan — bereavement@stcolumbatoronto.ca · 416-555-0142 ext. 31. Catholic Cemeteries also offers grief resources: catholic-cemeteries.ca.

Faith

Prayer and formation

A retreat day each Lent, the May crowning of Mary, the World Day of Prayer with neighbouring churches, and a monthly rosary for members who have died.

Service

Feeding and funding

Funeral receptions for grieving families (about forty a year), the November Christmas Bazaar & Bake Sale, layettes for new mothers through Rosalie Hall, and two $500 bursaries for graduating students.

Through the parish office when arranging the funeral. Sandwiches, sweets, tea and coffee for up to 150 for a suggested $250; waived in need.

item.title: Chaplaincies
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
When someone is in hospital, in a care home, in prison or living away from home at university, the Church goes to them. The Archdiocese of Toronto assigns priests, deacons and trained lay chaplains to institutions across the city, and every parish, including ours, shares in that care through its own pastoral visitors. This page explains what each chaplaincy does and, most importantly, how to reach one when you need it.

Hospital chaplaincy

Every major Toronto hospital has a spiritual care department, and Catholic chaplains, some of them priests, most of them trained lay ministers, deacons or religious sisters, work within it. A Catholic chaplain can bring Holy Communion, pray with you, arrange for a priest to hear your confession or anoint you, and sit with your family in difficult moments. Toronto also has a network of on-call priests so that anointing is available at any hour.

How to request a Catholic chaplain

  1. Tell the hospital you are Catholic

    Privacy law means the hospital will not tell any church who has been admitted. When you or your family member is registered, ask that "Roman Catholic" be recorded and that you would like a visit from the Catholic chaplain.

  2. Ask the nurse or the switchboard for Spiritual Care

    Any nurse can page the spiritual care department. Tell them what you need: Communion, a conversation, or a priest for anointing. Outside office hours the on-call priest is reached the same way.

  3. Let the parish know too

    Call the office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. We will add the name to the sick list if you wish, and one of our priests or Lay Pastoral Visitors will visit if the hospital is nearby.

Anointing of the Sick is not only for the dying

The sacrament is for anyone seriously ill, facing surgery or weakened by age, and it can be received more than once. Do not wait for the last hours. If you are going into hospital for a planned procedure, ask for anointing at St. Columba before you go. See Anointing of the Sick for details.

Long-term-care and home visits

Residents of nursing homes and retirement residences in our neighbourhood are visited by our clergy and Lay Pastoral Visitors on a monthly rotation, with a Communion service or Mass in the residence's common room. If your parent or spouse has moved into a care home anywhere in the Archdiocese, the parish that covers that address will take over visits; our office can make the introduction so no one falls through the cracks.

Parishioners who are housebound can receive Communion at home every week. Ask the office to arrange a Lay Pastoral Visitor, or speak to Deacon Ferreira after Mass.

University and college chaplaincy

The Archdiocese supports Catholic chaplaincies at the universities and colleges in Toronto, best known through the Newman Centre near the downtown campus, and through campus ministry teams at the other universities and colleges across the region. Chaplaincies offer Sunday and weekday Mass on or near campus, confession, retreats, faith-sharing groups, meals and a place to belong far from home. If a young person from our parish is heading to school this fall, encourage them to find the Catholic chaplaincy in the first week; students who connect early are far more likely to keep their faith through their studies.

Students home for the summer and Christmas are always welcome at our 5:00 PM Sunday youth and young adult Mass and at Young Adults events. Marcus Lee (youth@stcolumbatoronto.ca) can also connect students with campus ministers he knows.

Prison chaplaincy

Catholic chaplains serve the detention centres and correctional institutions in and around Toronto, celebrating Mass, leading Bible study and offering one-to-one support to inmates and, often, to their families. If a family member is incarcerated, they can ask to see the Catholic chaplain through the institution's chaplaincy office. Our St. Vincent de Paul conference also quietly supports families affected by incarceration; contact them through the office.

Our Lay Pastoral Visitors

St. Columba's Lay Pastoral Visitors are parishioners commissioned by the pastor to bring Holy Communion and the prayers of the parish to the sick, the housebound and residents of local care homes. There are currently fourteen visitors, and they serve about sixty people a month. Each has completed archdiocesan training, volunteer screening with a police vulnerable-sector check, and an annual refresher on privacy and boundaries.

  • What they do: a weekly or bi-weekly visit of 20 to 40 minutes, a short rite of Communion, prayer, and news from the parish, including the bulletin.
  • What they do not do: give medical or financial advice, handle money, or hear confessions; they will happily arrange a priest for those needs.
  • Who coordinates: Margaret Ferreira-Silva, pastoralcare@stcolumbatoronto.ca, through the parish office.

Would you like to become a visitor? We look for people who are steady, discreet and comfortable with silence. Training runs each October and February. See Volunteer and Volunteer Screening for what is involved.

Frequently asked

My mother is in hospital tonight. Who do I call for a priest?

Ask the nurse to page Spiritual Care and request the Catholic on-call priest; every Toronto hospital has one. Then call our office; if it is after hours, the voicemail gives the emergency number for our clergy.

Can a Lay Pastoral Visitor come to a retirement residence outside the parish?

Our visitors cover the residences within our parish boundaries. For others, we will contact that parish's pastoral care team on your behalf.

Is there a cost?

No. Chaplaincy and pastoral visiting are free. Families sometimes wish to make a donation to the parish afterwards, and that is welcome but never expected.

Questions? Contact the parish office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

Jesus told the disciples to let the children come, and we mean it. A restless toddler is the sound of the parish's future. Sit near the front where children can see; use the cry room at the back if you need a moment; and know that nobody is judging you.

Children's Liturgy of the Word

Sunday 11:00 AM Mass · ages 4–9 · September to June

After the opening prayer the children are invited to the chapel to hear the Sunday Gospel at their level, with a song and an activity, returning at the offertory. Parents may accompany children under five.

Catechesis of the Good Shepherd

Sundays 10:45 AM – 12:15 PM · ages 3–6 · atrium (room C)

A Montessori-based religious formation: children work quietly with beautiful materials — a model altar, a sheepfold, the parables — with trained catechists. Limited to 16 children; register in September.

Family Mass

1st Sunday · 9:00 AM

Children's choir, children as readers and gift-bearers, a homily aimed at families, and pancakes in the hall afterwards.

Cry room & nursery

Every Mass

A glassed room at the back with sound, rocking chairs and a change table. At the 11:00 AM Mass a supervised nursery for ages 1–3 runs in room B, staffed by screened volunteers.

Family events

Through the year

Blessing of backpacks (September), All Saints costume party, Advent wreath making, Christmas pageant, Easter egg hunt, June picnic.

Calendar

Sacraments

Baptism · First Communion · Confirmation

Programs and dates for each.

Sacramental preparation

Faith at home

What happens at home matters more than anything we do on Sunday. Small habits: grace before meals, a blessing on the forehead at bedtime, a crucifix and a picture of Mary where children can see them, the Sunday Gospel read together in the car. The parish's free FORMED subscription has children's videos and audio; ask the office for the parish code. Sr. Agnes runs a "Faith at Home" parents' evening each October.

Practical notes

  • Change tables in the accessible washroom and the cry room; a bottle warmer in the nursery.
  • Strollers may be parked in the narthex; the side aisles are wide enough to bring them in.
  • Children's bulletins and crayons are at the doors.
  • All volunteers with children have completed screening; children are only ever with two adults.
  • Pick up children from the atrium and nursery with the numbered tag you were given.

Questions

At what age can my child be an altar server or join the choir?

Altar servers from Grade 3 (after First Communion); the children's choir from Grade 2. See altar servers and music.

Is there a parish school?

Yes — St. Columba Catholic School (TCDSB) is two blocks away; see parish school.

How can parents help?

Children's liturgy leaders, nursery volunteers, pancake cooks and pageant costume-makers are always needed — an hour a month. See volunteer.

item.title: Confirmation
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
In Confirmation the Holy Spirit, first given at Baptism, is sealed and strengthened in a young person so that they can live and share their faith as an adult member of the Church. In the Archdiocese of Toronto it is normally celebrated in Grade 7.

Requirements

  • Baptized Catholic, in Grade 7 or older, who has made First Communion (if not, we prepare for both — please call).
  • Attendance at all monthly sessions and the retreat; one session may be made up.
  • Regular Sunday Mass with the family through the year.
  • Ten hours of service — at the parish (pantry, picnic, Coffee Sunday, altar serving) or in the community — recorded on the service sheet.
  • A short letter to the pastor, written by the candidate, asking to be confirmed and saying why.

Choosing a sponsor and a name

The sponsor stands with the candidate and promises to support them in living the faith. A sponsor must be a confirmed, practising Catholic at least 16 years old — a godparent is ideal, and a parent may not be the sponsor. Sponsors provide a letter of good standing from their parish. Candidates may take a confirmation name: the name of a saint whose story they have read and want to imitate. Many keep their baptismal name if it is already a saint's.

The celebration

The Bishop (or his delegate) celebrates Mass at 3:00 PM. After the homily the candidates renew their baptismal promises; then each comes forward with their sponsor's hand on their shoulder. The Bishop anoints the forehead with chrism, saying "Name, be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit," and the candidate answers "Amen." Candidates wear a red gown provided by the parish over neat clothes. Families may invite as many guests as they wish; a reception with the Bishop follows in the hall.

Adults

Baptized Catholics who were never confirmed — often because they moved, or simply missed it — are confirmed at the Easter Vigil or at Pentecost after a short preparation with the OCIA group from January. Many are engaged couples who want to be confirmed before marriage, or parents preparing to be godparents. See Becoming Catholic or call Sr. Agnes.

Questions

My child goes to a public school.

The parish program is the same for everyone; nothing depends on the school. All candidates prepare together.

What if my child is not sure they want to be confirmed?

Honesty is good. Come to the first meeting anyway; the program is designed for questions. Nobody is confirmed against their will, and anyone can be confirmed later, at any age.

Is there a fee?

$60 covers the candidate book, retreat, gown and reception; waived on request.

item.title: Cultural Communities
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Toronto is the most multicultural city in the world, and a Toronto parish looks like it. Founded by Irish and Italian families, St. Columba now prays in six languages. Language Masses are not separate parishes; they are the same community praying in its mother tongue, and every parishioner is welcome at every Mass.

  • English
  • Español
  • Tagalog
  • Italiano
  • Português
  • தமிழ்

Comunidad hispana

Spanish-speaking community

Mass in Spanish: 1st and 3rd Sundays, 1:00 PM, with the Coro Hispano. Renovación Carismática: Tuesdays 7:00 PM in the hall. Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on December 12 with mañanitas at 6:00 AM, Mass and a fiesta; Via Crucis viviente on Good Friday; Alpha en español in January. About 200 families from Colombia, Mexico, El Salvador, Peru and Venezuela.

Contact: Carlos Mendoza · hispana@stcolumbatoronto.ca

Filipino community

Simbahan ng mga Pilipino

Mass in Tagalog: 2nd Sunday, 1:00 PM. Bukas Loob sa Diyos prayer community after the Mass. Simbang Gabi: nine dawn Masses from December 16 to 24 at 6:00 AM with breakfast after; Santo Niño feast in January; Flores de Mayo. The community also runs the Sunday 5:00 PM supper once a month.

Contact: Marlene Aquino · filipino@stcolumbatoronto.ca

Comunità italiana

Italian community

Mass in Italian: 4th Sunday, 1:00 PM. Padre Pio Prayer Group: 3rd Sunday after Mass. Feast of San Rocco in August with a procession and a pasta lunch; the Christmas presepio in the church since 1963. The community founded the parish in 1954 alongside the Irish, and its seniors are the backbone of the Wednesday Prime Time club.

Contact: Giuseppe Rossi · italiana@stcolumbatoronto.ca

Comunidade portuguesa

Portuguese community

Mass in Portuguese on the first Sunday of May and October at 3:00 PM, with the candlelight procession of Our Lady of Fátima in May; the rosary in Portuguese on the 13th of each month at 7:00 PM. Confessions in Portuguese by appointment with Fr. Moreau.

Contact: Maria de Sousa · portuguesa@stcolumbatoronto.ca

Tamil community

Tamil Catholic community

An annual Mass in Tamil for the feast of Our Lady of Madhu in August, a Tamil rosary group on Saturday evenings, and a growing group of young families from Sri Lanka and India who serve at the 11:00 AM Mass. A visiting Tamil-speaking priest hears confessions in Advent and Lent.

Contact: Anthony Selvaraj · tamil@stcolumbatoronto.ca

Everyone

International Mass & potluck

On Pentecost Sunday the 11:00 AM Mass is celebrated with readings and hymns in all six languages, followed by the parish's most popular lunch of the year. Each community also takes a turn hosting Coffee Sunday.

New communities

Toronto changes, and so does the parish. If there is a group of parishioners who share a language and would like a Mass, a devotion or a feast celebrated, speak to Fr. Moreau. The parish can often find a visiting priest through the Archdiocese's ethnic chaplaincies, and the hall and church are made available without charge. In the past five years we have added the Tamil rosary group and Simbang Gabi; the next community is probably already sitting in the pews.

Questions

Can I go to a language Mass if I don't speak the language?

Of course. The Mass is the same everywhere; bilingual missalettes are at the door, and the homily is often summarized in English.

Are sacraments available in other languages?

Baptisms and weddings can be celebrated bilingually in Spanish, Tagalog, Italian and Portuguese; confessions are heard in Spanish, Italian and Portuguese by our priests.

I am a newcomer to Canada.

Welcome. The community contacts above can connect you with people from home, and the St. Vincent de Paul conference and refugee committee can help with settlement questions.

item.title: First Reconciliation & First Communion
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Receiving Jesus in the Eucharist for the first time is one of the great days of a Catholic childhood. Preparation is a partnership: the parish provides the sessions and the celebration, the Catholic school reinforces it in class, and parents — the first teachers of the faith — do the most important part at home and at Sunday Mass.

Who can register

Children in Grade 2 or older who have been baptized. Children attending St. Columba Catholic School register with the parish as well as the school; children in public or other schools are fully welcome and receive the same sessions. Older children and teenagers who missed First Communion prepare in a small group with Sr. Agnes — please call rather than register online.

What families do at home

  • Come to Sunday Mass together — every week, not just during the program.
  • Work through the family book, a chapter a month (about twenty minutes).
  • Pray together at meals and bedtime; learn the Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be and the Act of Contrition.
  • Talk about your own First Communion and why the Eucharist matters to you.

The celebrations

First Reconciliation is gentle and short. The children gather with their families for a reading and an examination of conscience, then go one by one to a priest, face to face, while the others sing. Parents are encouraged to go to confession the same morning. First Communion is celebrated within the 11:00 AM Sunday Mass. Children sit together at the front with their families behind; each child receives Communion from the pastor, and there is a blessing of parents at the end. A photographer records the Mass so that families can be present rather than behind a phone; portraits are taken afterwards on the front steps.

Dress and guests

Girls traditionally wear white dresses and boys a white shirt with dark trousers, but anything neat and modest is fine; nobody is judged by a dress. Each family may invite as many guests as they like — reserved seating is for the child and two adults. A reception with cake in the hall follows.

Questions

Our child was baptized in another parish or country.

Bring a copy of the baptism certificate — any language is fine. If it is lost, tell us the parish and year and we will help you request it.

We cannot attend the Sunday sessions.

Speak to Sr. Agnes; a Tuesday evening group runs for families who work Sundays.

Is there a fee?

A contribution of $40 covers the family book, the retreat and the reception. It is waived on request, no questions asked.

My child has a food allergy or coeliac disease.

Low-gluten hosts are available for children with coeliac disease, and Communion may be received from the chalice alone. Tell us at registration.

item.title: Funerals & Bereavement
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
First steps

If a death is expected or has just happened, call the parish at 416-555-0142 (press 9 outside office hours) so that a priest can come to pray with the family. Then contact a funeral home; they will call us to arrange the date.

A Catholic funeral does three things: it commends the person who has died to God's mercy, it gives thanks for their life, and it gathers the living to grieve with hope. The parish celebrates about forty funerals a year. There is no such thing as a family too small, a person too unknown or a death too difficult for the Church to bury with dignity.

The three moments

  1. The vigil

    Usually the evening before, at the funeral home or in the church: Scripture, prayers and, if the family wishes, the rosary and words of remembrance. This is the natural place for eulogies, photographs and music that would not suit the Mass.

  2. The funeral Mass

    In the church, usually at 10:00 or 11:00 AM on a weekday, occasionally Saturday morning. The body or the cremated remains are received at the door, sprinkled with water and covered with the white pall recalling baptism. The Mass includes readings chosen by the family, a homily, the Eucharist and the final commendation. About an hour. A funeral Liturgy outside Mass is also possible, led by a deacon.

  3. The committal

    At the cemetery or crematorium: a short rite of prayers as the body is laid to rest. Many families choose one of the Archdiocese's Catholic cemeteries — Catholic Cemeteries & Funeral Services — which offer pre-planning at no obligation.

Planning the Mass

The priest or deacon meets the family, usually the day after the death, to plan. You will choose two readings and a psalm from a booklet we provide, and family members may proclaim them. The Director of Music helps choose hymns — sacred music is used within the Mass, while secular songs belong at the vigil or reception. One family member may offer a few words of remembrance (three to four minutes, written down) before the final commendation. Photographs and a memorial table are welcome in the narthex.

Practical questions

Cremation

The Church permits cremation. Where possible the funeral Mass takes place with the body present, followed by cremation; the ashes are then buried or entombed in a cemetery or columbarium, kept together, not scattered or divided. Our parish columbarium niches in the memorial garden are available to parishioners; ask the office.

Offerings

The customary offering to the parish is $350 for the funeral Mass, and $250 for the musicians, both usually arranged through the funeral home. They are waived without question for families in need. The priest's stipend is included.

The person who died was not a practising Catholic, or died by suicide.

Any baptized Catholic may have a Catholic funeral, whatever their practice; the Church also buries the non-Catholic spouse or child of a Catholic family. The Church entrusts every death — including death by suicide — to the mercy of God, and prays for the person without judgment.

Can the funeral be livestreamed?

Yes, at no cost, with a private link for relatives who cannot travel. Ask when planning.

Reception

The Catholic Women's League offers a light reception (sandwiches, sweets, tea and coffee) in the parish hall after the funeral for a modest charge; book it through the office.

Afterwards

Grief does not end at the cemetery gate. Our Bereavement Ministry offers an eight-week support group each spring and fall, one-to-one companions, and a Mass of Remembrance on All Souls' Day (November 2) to which every family we have buried in the past year is invited. You can have a Mass offered on the anniversary, and the parish prays for the recently deceased at every weekend Mass in the month after the funeral.

Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen.

58% ministry, staff & liturgy

The Finance Council publishes a full annual report each spring; a summary is on the Parish Councils page and printed copies are at the back of the church. Roughly speaking, $25 a week from a family covers that family's share of heating, lighting and insurance; anything above that builds ministry.

Give time and talent too

Money is one gift of three. The parish runs on volunteers: lectors, counters, gardeners, pantry sorters, catechists, drivers. If your budget is tight this year, an hour a week is just as welcome.

Yes. One receipt for all your gifts of the calendar year is mailed (or emailed) by the end of February. St. Columba Parish is a registered charity (no. 10000 0000 RR0001 — placeholder). Online gifts are receipted by the Archdiocese.

The portal is operated by the Archdiocese of Toronto and processes cards through a PCI-compliant provider. The parish never sees or stores your card number.

Yes: building fund, organ fund, St. Vincent de Paul, youth ministry and refugee sponsorship all accept designated gifts. Undesignated gifts go to the general operating fund, which is where the need is greatest.

Why does the parish pay an assessment to the Archdiocese?

The assessment supports seminary formation, retired priests, chancery services and poorer parishes. It is calculated on ordinary income and audited annually.

item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
St. Columba's parish hall sits on the lower level of the church, reached by the east-side accessible entrance and elevator or by the interior stairs from the vestibule. Renovated in 2019, it has a sprung hardwood floor, a stage, a full commercial kitchen and seating for 220 at round tables or 300 in rows. Parish groups use it most weekday evenings, but weekends and daytimes are often available for families and community groups. Baptism and First Communion receptions, wedding receptions, funeral luncheons, milestone birthdays, cultural association gatherings and neighbourhood meetings all find a home here.

The space

  • Main hall: about 4,200 square feet, 12-foot ceilings, hardwood floor, seating for 220 at tables (24 round tables of 8 to 10) or 300 in theatre rows.
  • Stage: 24 by 14 feet with a ramp, stage lighting, a lectern and a sound system with two wireless microphones; a projector and 12-foot screen are available.
  • Kitchen: commercial six-burner range, two ovens, warming cabinet, two fridges, a chest freezer, dishwasher and ample counter space. Suitable for caterers or for cooking on site.
  • Bar area with a service counter and ice machine.
  • Accessible: level entry from the elevator, accessible washroom, wide doors, ramp to the stage; see Accessibility.
  • Meeting room: a separate 30-seat room beside the hall, available on its own for smaller gatherings.
  • Parking for 60 cars in the church lot, plus street parking.

Rates

Rates are set by the Finance Council and reviewed each January. A registered parishioner is anyone whose household is on our parish roll; see Register with the Parish. Funeral luncheons for parishioners are offered at no charge (a donation is welcome).

Registered not-for-profit community groups may request the parishioner rate. A $100 non-refundable deposit confirms your date; the balance and the damage deposit are due 14 days before the event. Payment by cheque, e-transfer or debit at the office.

What is included

Every booking includes tables and chairs (set up by our custodian to your floor plan, submitted a week ahead), the sound system and microphones, use of washrooms and the coat room, heating and air conditioning, and a walk-through with Luis Ortega, our custodian, before the event. Tablecloths, dishes and cutlery are not included; caterers usually supply these, or you may rent our stock of 220 white place settings for $1.50 per setting.

Rules for renters

  1. Alcohol

    Alcohol may be served only with a Special Occasion Permit from the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, obtained by the renter and posted at the event, and only by a Smart Serve certified bartender. A copy of the permit must be on file at the office seven days before the event. No alcohol may be sold without the permit's sale endorsement.

  2. Insurance

    Non-parishioner renters and any event serving alcohol must provide a certificate of liability insurance for $2 million naming St. Columba Parish and the Archdiocese of Toronto as additional insureds. Event insurance for a single day is available from most brokers for roughly $100 to $200, and the office can suggest providers.

  3. Hours and noise

    Music ends at 11:30 PM and the hall must be vacated by midnight. Our neighbours are close; please keep the east doors closed during amplified music.

  4. Cleanup

    Renters remove all decorations, food and garbage (bagged and placed in the bins in the loading area), wipe tables, and leave the kitchen as they found it. Our custodian handles floors and washrooms. The damage deposit is returned within two weeks if the hall is left in good order.

  5. Respect for the space

    The hall is part of a church. No open flames other than sternos, no confetti or glitter, no tape or tacks on painted walls (use the hanging rails), no smoking or cannabis anywhere on the property, and no events that conflict with Catholic teaching or the parish's mission. The pastor has the final say on any booking.

Availability

The hall is not available on Sunday mornings, during Holy Week, or on Christmas Eve and Day. Saturday evenings book up three to six months ahead, and June and December are our busiest months. Parish groups have first call on weekday evenings.

How to book

  1. Send an inquiry using the form below, or call Ann Marie O'Connor at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. Tell us the date, the kind of event and the expected numbers.
  2. We confirm availability within two business days and invite you to see the hall.
  3. Sign the rental agreement and pay the $100 deposit to hold the date.
  4. Submit your floor plan, permit and insurance certificate at least 7 days before the event, and pay the balance 14 days before.
  5. Meet the custodian on the day for keys and a walk-through.

Hall rental inquiry

Inquiries go to the parish office. We reply within two business days. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Thank you. Your inquiry has been received and the office will be in touch within two business days.

Frequently asked

Can we bring our own caterer?

Yes. Any licensed caterer is welcome, and we can suggest several that know the kitchen. Caterers must be out and the kitchen clean by the end of your booking.

Can we come the day before to decorate?

If the hall is free, decorating time can be booked at the weekday daytime rate. Please ask when you book.

Is the hall available for non-Catholic groups?

Yes, for community events consistent with the parish's mission. Political fundraisers and events with content contrary to Church teaching are not accepted.

Questions? Contact Ann Marie O'Connor at 416-555-0142 ext. 20 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca.
