item.title: Parish History
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Every parish is a story of people who decided that a church belonged where they lived. At St. Columba the story begins in the years after the Second World War, when East York's market gardens were giving way to streets of new brick houses and the families moving into them, many of them fresh off the boat from Cork, Calabria and Kerry, had a long walk to the nearest Catholic church. What follows is the short version. The long version lives in the memories of our older parishioners, and we are collecting it.

Timeline

  • 1954

    A parish is founded

    The Archbishop of Toronto established St. Columba Parish on September 12, 1954, carving it out of the territory of two older parishes. The first pastor, Fr. Michael Brennan, celebrated the first Mass on the following Sunday in the rented Orange Hall on Pape Avenue, an irony the Irish founders enjoyed for years. About 180 families registered in the first month.

  • 1956

    The parish hall

    Land on Columba Avenue was purchased and a plain cinder-block hall went up, built largely by volunteers on Saturdays. It served as church, school gym and social centre for five years, with Mass at the front and bingo at the back on Fridays.

  • 1961

    The church is dedicated

    The present church, designed in a modern Gothic style with a 32-metre bell tower, was dedicated on May 21, 1961. Parishioners paid for it with a building campaign that took seven years to retire; the Italian community donated the marble altar, and the Catholic Women's League furnished the sacristy.

  • 1970s

    Portuguese and Italian growth

    Immigration from the Azores and southern Italy changed the neighbourhood, and the parish with it. Sunday Mass in Italian began in 1972, and a Portuguese-speaking assistant priest arrived in 1976. The feast of Our Lady of Fátima procession, still held each May, dates from these years.

  • 1984

    Thirtieth anniversary

    The church was repainted, the pipe organ installed, and the parish choir formally founded under its first director. The St. Vincent de Paul conference opened its food cupboard in the hall basement.

  • 1990s

    Filipino and Spanish communities

    Newcomers from the Philippines, Colombia, El Salvador and Peru made the parish home. Mass in Tagalog began in 1993 and in Spanish in 1997. The Legion of Mary and the Simbang Gabi novena before Christmas both trace their beginnings here to this decade.

  • 2004

    Golden jubilee renovation

    For the fiftieth anniversary the sanctuary was reordered, the roof replaced and the stained glass restored. The Archbishop celebrated the jubilee Mass on September 12, 2004, exactly fifty years after the founding.

  • 2019

    Accessibility project

    A $1.4 million campaign funded the east-side accessible entrance, an elevator to the hall, accessible washrooms and a hearing loop, making every part of the parish available to every parishioner. Fr. Daniel Moreau arrived as pastor the same summer.

  • 2020–2021

    The pandemic

    With the church closed for long stretches, the parish learned to livestream Mass, deliver groceries to seniors and run Confirmation classes online. The livestream continues every Sunday at 11:00 AM.

  • 2024

    Seventieth anniversary

    Seventy years to the day after the first Mass, the parish gathered for a bilingual anniversary Mass, a photo exhibition in the hall and a dinner that sold out its 220 seats in a week. A Tamil community, the sixth language group, was formally welcomed the same year.

The church building

The church seats 540 and was built in a restrained modern Gothic style typical of Toronto parishes of the early 1960s: a tall brick nave, a narrow bell tower, and clear light from high windows. The three bells were cast in 1961 and are named for the founding pastor's parents and for St. Columba himself.

The stained glass, installed in stages between 1961 and 1974, tells the life of Christ down the north aisle and the lives of saints of the parish's founding nations down the south: Patrick, Brigid, Francis of Assisi, Anthony of Padua, Columba. A window of Our Lady of Fátima was added by the Portuguese community in 1980, and one of San Lorenzo Ruiz by the Filipino community in 2004.

Pastors of St. Columba

Help us keep the story

Parish archive project

We are gathering photographs, bulletins, wedding programs and memories from the parish's first decades. If you have a shoebox of pictures from a First Communion in 1965 or the hall's opening in 1956, we would love to scan them and give them back the same day. Contact the office at 416-555-0142 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca. Selected images appear in the photo gallery.

The parish's sacramental registers, which go back to the first baptism in October 1954, are kept in the office. If you need a baptism, confirmation or marriage certificate, see Questions & Answers for how to request one.

item.title: Holy Orders
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Through Holy Orders a baptized man is configured to Christ in a particular way — to teach, to sanctify and to shepherd the people of God. It is conferred in three degrees by the laying on of hands and the prayer of a bishop, in a line that stretches back to the apostles.

Fullness of Orders

Bishop

A successor of the apostles who leads a diocese, ordains priests and deacons, and confirms. The Archbishop of Toronto shepherds about two million Catholics in 225 parishes.

Co-worker of the bishop

Priest

Celebrates the Eucharist, forgives sins, anoints the sick, preaches and leads a parish. Diocesan priests, like ours, promise celibacy, obedience to the bishop and a life of prayer.

Ordained for service

Deacon

Proclaims the Gospel, preaches, baptizes, witnesses marriages, presides at funerals outside Mass and serves the poor. Permanent deacons are usually married men with careers; our Deacon Paul Ferreira is a retired teacher.

Exploring a call

A vocation rarely arrives as a bolt of lightning. It is usually a quiet, persistent question — "could I?" — that grows in prayer, is tested by wise people, and is confirmed by the Church. If you are asking the question, you are already discerning. Some next steps:

  1. Talk to a priest

    Fr. Moreau and Fr. Nguyen are glad to have a conversation, without commitment. So is Deacon Paul, for men considering the diaconate.

  2. Pray and serve

    Daily Mass when you can, adoration on Thursdays, confession regularly, and a ministry — altar serving, the pantry, youth ministry — where you serve people rather than talk about serving them.

  3. Contact the Vocations Office

    The Archdiocese's Office of Vocations runs discernment evenings, "Come and See" weekends at St. Augustine's Seminary and a Quo Vadis retreat for young men. See vocationstoronto.ca and our vocations page.

  4. Formation

    Seminary formation for the priesthood takes six to eight years, including philosophy, theology and pastoral placements. Permanent deacons are formed over four years of evening and weekend study with their wives' involvement, applying through their pastor after age 35.

Sons of the parish

St. Columba has given the Church four priests and two permanent deacons since 1954: Fr. Kevin Doyle (ordained 1971), Fr. Antonio Ferraro (1988), Fr. Mark Osei (2009) and Fr. Paul Tran (2021), and Deacons Frank Costa (1999) and Paul Ferreira (2015). Their photographs hang in the parish hall. We pray for vocations at every weekend Mass, and the Serra Club sponsors a seminarian each year.

A prayer for vocations

Lord Jesus, you called the apostles to leave their nets and follow you. Call from our parish generous hearts to serve your Church as priests, deacons, sisters and brothers. Give those you call the courage to answer, and give us the faith to support them. Mary, Mother of the Church, pray for us. Amen.

Can married men become priests?

In the Latin Church, priests are ordained from among unmarried men who promise celibacy, with rare exceptions for former ministers of other traditions. Married men may be ordained permanent deacons.

What about women?

The Church teaches that it cannot ordain women. Women lead much of the parish's life — Sr. Agnes coordinates all our faith formation — and the Church's religious sisters, lay ministers and theologians are vocations in their own right; see our vocations page.

Research on why people stay in a parish keeps finding the same thing: it is not the homily or the music, it is whether someone spoke to them. Hospitality ministry makes sure someone does. Greeters

Every Mass · at the doors from 20 minutes before

Say good morning, hand out the bulletin, notice the person who looks lost, point out the washrooms and the cry room. Once a month.

Ushers

Every Mass · four per Mass

Seat latecomers, take up the collection, guide the Communion procession, assist anyone unwell (all ushers take a first-aid orientation and know where the defibrillator is), and tidy the pews after.

1st Sunday · after the 9:00 and 11:00 AM Masses · hall

Coffee, tea, juice and baking. Teams of five set up, serve and clean up; cultural communities take turns hosting with their own food. The best hour of the parish month.

Sundays · narthex, after each Mass

Registration forms, envelope boxes, ministry information, Mass intention books and a person who can answer "how do I…?"

As needed · with the CWL

The newcomers' supper

Four times a year, on a Sunday evening after the 5:00 PM Mass, Fr. Moreau hosts supper in the hall for everyone who has registered in the past three months — about twenty households each time. If you like people, you are qualified. Greeters and ushers serve at the Mass they already attend, once a month; training is a single evening. From Grade 9, with an adult usher at the same Mass; it counts for service hours.

Founded in 1882 by Blessed Michael McGivney, a parish priest, to protect Catholic families, the Knights of Columbus is the world's largest Catholic fraternal organization. Our council was chartered in 1961 and has about 140 members, from twenty-somethings to a 94-year-old charter member who still comes to meetings.

What the Knights do here

Charity

Raising and giving

The October Charity Dinner & Dance ($60 a ticket, 200 guests) funds the St. Vincent de Paul pantry and Special Olympics Ontario. Coats for Kids each November; the Christmas hamper drive; a $1,000 bursary for a graduating parish student.

Parish

Hands and grills

The Knights run the barbecue at the picnic, the pancake breakfasts, the Good Friday Stations outdoors, snow-clearing on Sunday mornings and an annual work day that repaints what the budget cannot reach.

Faith & family

Growing as men

A monthly men's Holy Hour, the Into the Breach video series, a father-son campout in June, and the Knights' insurance and fraternal benefits for members' families.

Joining

Any practising Catholic man aged 18 or older may join. The simplest route is to come to a meeting at 7:00 PM on the second Monday, or to join online at kofc.org and choose Council 12345. New members take the Exemplification of Charity, Unity and Fraternity — a thirty-minute ceremony now held at the parish several times a year, to which families are welcome. The Fourth Degree (patriotic) and the Colour Corps, whose members in regalia serve at funerals and Confirmation, are open after a year.

Questions

How much time does it take?

As much or as little as you have. A member who comes to the monthly meeting and helps at two events a year is a full member. Many retired Knights give a morning a week.

Is it a secret society?

No. The ceremonies have been public since 2020, the finances are reported to the parish, and the pastor is the council's chaplain.

Can my wife or daughter take part?

Membership is for men, but almost every event is a family event, and the Knights and the CWL run the bazaar, receptions and dinner together.

What is the insurance program?

The Knights' own life insurance and retirement products, available to members and their families through a field agent; no obligation to buy anything.

item.title: Legion of Mary
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The Legion of Mary was founded in Dublin in 1921 by Frank Duff and is now in almost every country on earth. Members — "legionaries" — commit to a weekly meeting and a weekly assignment of active work, done in pairs, under the guidance of Mary. Our praesidium, Our Lady of Knock, was founded in 1959 and has eighteen active members and about seventy auxiliaries who support the work by prayer.

Meeting

  • Mondays7:00 PM
  • Meeting room B
  • About 75 minutes

Membership

  • Activemeeting + 2 hours' work weekly
  • Auxiliarydaily prayers only
  • Juniorages 10–17, Saturdays

Contact

  • President: Josephine Okonkwo
  • legion@stcolumbatoronto.ca
  • Spiritual director: Fr. Nguyen

The meeting

Every praesidium in the world follows the same order: the opening prayers and the rosary, a short spiritual reading, reports from each pair on the week's work (five minutes each, and confidential), an allocutio — a brief talk by the spiritual director — the assignment of next week's work, and the closing prayers. A secret bag collection covers expenses. The structure is old-fashioned and the effect is remarkable: people who joined for the prayer find they have become visitors of the sick.

The work

  • Visiting the housebound and the residents of the two long-term-care homes, praying the rosary with them, and bringing Communion where a member is a commissioned minister.
  • Hospital visits to parishioners at the local hospital, in cooperation with the Catholic chaplain.
  • Calling on newly registered parishioners with a welcome pack, and on families after a baptism or funeral.
  • Door-to-door visits in the parish each May and October, inviting lapsed Catholics back — gently.
  • Leading the rosary before weekday Mass and at wakes, and organizing the May crowning and the October rosary rally.
  • Enrolling children in the Miraculous Medal and the Brown Scapular after First Communion.

Joining

Come to a Monday meeting as a guest — there is no commitment for the first three months, after which a new member makes the Legionary Promise. Active members must be practising Catholics who have made their First Communion; all complete high-risk screening because the work is with vulnerable people. Auxiliary members promise the daily Legion prayers (the Catena and rosary) and are invited to the annual Acies in March and the Christmas social. A junior praesidium for ages 10–17 meets on Saturdays at 10:30 AM and helps with the children's rosary and the Christmas hamper deliveries.

How much time is it really?

The meeting plus about two hours of work a week, usually one visit with your partner. Members who travel or fall ill simply report it; the Legion has been doing this for a century and understands life.

I'm shy about knocking on doors.

Most legionaries were. Work is always done in pairs, new members go with experienced ones, and there are plenty of works that involve no doors at all.

Josephine Okonkwo, President — legion@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

If illness, age, distance or a newborn keeps you at home, you can still pray with your parish. Our Sunday 11:00 AM Mass and the weekday 8:30 AM Mass are streamed live, and each recording remains on our channel for a month.

  • 11:00 AM MassSun

Watch later

  • Recordingskept 30 days

  • Parish eventsconcerts, talks

How to watch

  1. On this page

    The player above switches to the live stream a few minutes before Mass begins. Press play; if it says "waiting", refresh the page at the start time.

  2. On YouTube

    Open the parish YouTube channel (demo link) and choose the "Live" tab. Subscribe and turn on notifications to be told when a stream starts.

  3. On a television

    Open the YouTube app on a smart TV, Apple TV, Roku or Chromecast, search for the channel name and choose the live video. Larger text and a bigger picture make this the best option for older parishioners.

Praying along at home

Set the room up as you would a pew: sit up, put the phone away, light a candle if you can. Say the responses out loud. The readings for the day are at Living with Christ. At Communion, when you cannot receive, pray the Act of Spiritual Communion:

My Jesus, I believe that you are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love you above all things, and I desire to receive you into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive you sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace you as if you were already there and unite myself wholly to you. Never permit me to be separated from you. Amen.

Act of Spiritual Communion, St. Alphonsus Liguori

If you are unable to come to church for a long period, please tell the office: a Lay Pastoral Visitor can bring Holy Communion to your home each week.

Questions

The video says "This live stream is offline."

The stream usually starts five minutes before Mass. If it is still offline at the start time, refresh the page; if the problem continues, a recording will be posted within the hour.

Does watching online fulfil the Sunday obligation?

No — the obligation is to take part in Mass in person. Those who are sick, caring for the sick, or otherwise unable to attend are excused from the obligation, and the livestream is offered for them.

Can we stream a funeral or wedding for relatives overseas?

Yes. Ask when you arrange the celebration; there is no charge, and the link can be private.

Will I appear on camera?

The camera shows the sanctuary and the back of the congregation from a distance. If you prefer not to be visible at all, sit in the side pews, which are out of frame.

On the WordPress version of this site the video is a standard YouTube embed block that the office can point at any video or live stream.

item.title: Marriage & Family Life
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The family is the first church a child ever knows. Supporting marriages — before, during and when they are in trouble — is some of the most important work a parish does, and most of it is done by other couples and parents rather than by clergy.

Marriage preparation

Weekend courses · February and October

Required for couples marrying in the Church, led by three married couples and a priest: communication, finances, faith, intimacy, children. $150 per couple with meals.

Getting married

Couples for Christ — St. Columba

2nd Saturday · 7:00 PM · hall

A Catholic family renewal community with roots in the Philippines and members from every background: household groups of five or six couples meeting fortnightly, a monthly assembly with praise and teaching, and a Christian Life Program each January for new couples. Singles for Christ and Youth for Christ for the rest of the family.

Contact: Ricardo & Elena Santos · cfc@stcolumbatoronto.ca

Moms' group

Thursdays 9:30 AM · meeting room A · babies and toddlers welcome

Coffee, a short reflection, honest conversation, and a room full of toys. Grandmothers on hand to hold babies.

Dads' group

1st Saturday · 7:30 AM · breakfast in the hall

Forty-five minutes: bacon, the Sunday Gospel, and what it means to be a father this week. Out by 8:30 for the kids' hockey.

Family rosary

1st Friday · 6:30 PM · before Adoration

Children lead the decades; a Marian hymn; then pizza while parents stay for Adoration. In October, every night.

Anniversaries Mass

Sunday nearest June 21 · 11:00 AM · reception after

Couples celebrating 1, 5, 10, 25, 40, 50, 60 or more years renew their vows and receive a blessing and certificate. Register by June 1.

Enrichment

Marriages need maintenance the way houses do. The parish offers an annual marriage enrichment evening in February (dinner, a speaker, time to talk as a couple), promotes Worldwide Marriage Encounter weekends, and keeps a small library of books on marriage in the parish library. Fr. Moreau and Deacon Paul are available for couples who want to talk something through before it becomes a crisis. Natural Family Planning instruction is offered by a certified parishioner couple; ask the office.

When marriage is hard, or has ended

Couples in difficulty can be referred by the priests to Catholic Family Services of Toronto for counselling (sliding scale; ShareLife-funded) and to Retrouvaille, a weekend program for marriages in serious trouble that has saved many. Separated and divorced Catholics remain full members of the Church and are welcome at Communion; the parish hosts a monthly Separated & Divorced Catholics support evening on the third Wednesday, and the priests can explain the annulment process, which is confidential and free in the Archdiocese of Toronto. Single parents are especially invited to the moms' and dads' groups and to the family events.

Questions

We're an interfaith couple.

Every group on this page is open to you both. Couples for Christ and marriage enrichment have several mixed-faith couples.

Is there childcare at the groups?

Children come to the moms' group and the family rosary; for the Saturday CFC assembly there is a supervised kids' program. Dads' breakfast is for dads.

We were married civilly.

See convalidation — a simple ceremony that brings your marriage into the Church.

item.title: Marriage
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
A Catholic wedding is a sacrament: the couple themselves are its ministers, promising before God and the Church a love that is free, faithful, total and open to life. We would be honoured to celebrate yours. The parish celebrates about thirty weddings a year, on Saturdays at 11:00 AM, 1:00 PM and 3:00 PM and on Friday afternoons.

  1. Call the office — a year ahead

    Before booking a hall. Ann Marie will arrange a first meeting with one of the priests within two weeks, where the date is pencilled in.

  2. First meeting with the priest

    Getting to know you, confirming you are both free to marry, and going over the steps. Bring identification and, if either of you was married before (civilly or in any church), the relevant documents — please tell us at this stage.

  3. Documents

    New baptism certificates for each Catholic party (issued within six months of the wedding), confirmation details, and a Prenuptial Enquiry completed with the priest. Two witnesses who have known each of you for years complete freedom-to-marry affidavits. An Ontario marriage licence (City Hall, valid 90 days) is required before the rehearsal.

  4. Marriage preparation course

    Required in the Archdiocese of Toronto. The parish runs a weekend course in February and October ($150 per couple, including meals); archdiocesan and Catholic Family Services courses are also accepted. Couples also complete a FOCCUS or Prepare-Enrich inventory and discuss it with the priest.

  5. Planning the ceremony

    Two months out you choose the readings, music (with the Director of Music), whether the wedding is within Mass (for two Catholics) or a Liturgy of the Word, and the readers. The rehearsal is usually two days before.

Mixed and interfaith marriages

A Catholic may marry a baptized Christian of another tradition (a "mixed marriage") or a person of another faith or none. The wedding is normally celebrated outside Mass so that everyone can take part fully; the non-Catholic party's minister may be invited to offer a blessing or reading. The Catholic promises to continue practising the faith and to do all they can to raise children as Catholics; the other party is informed of that promise but makes no promise. The priest obtains the needed permission from the Archdiocese.

Already married civilly?

Couples who married at City Hall or elsewhere can have their marriage recognized by the Church in a simple ceremony called a convalidation, often with close family present. The preparation is shorter and the priest will explain it in one meeting. Many couples do this before a child's baptism or their own confirmation.

If either of you has been married before, a previous marriage must be examined by the Church before a new one can be celebrated. The priest will explain the annulment process of the Marriage Tribunal of the Archdiocese; it is confidential, costs nothing in Toronto, and usually takes twelve to eighteen months, so please begin early.

Offerings and practical matters

Photographers and videographers are welcome and receive a one-page guide at the rehearsal; they may not enter the sanctuary during the ceremony. The church seats 420. Weddings are not celebrated on Sundays, during the Easter Triduum or on Christmas Eve or Day.

Questions

We live outside the parish.

If either of you grew up here or your family are parishioners, we are glad to celebrate your wedding. Otherwise your own parish is the normal place — but call us and we will help you find the right arrangement.

Can we write our own vows?

The vows are the words of the Church's rite, in one of two approved forms. You may add personal words in the program or at the reception.

Can we marry outdoors or at a venue?

Catholic weddings are celebrated in a church. A blessing at a reception venue afterwards can be arranged.

How long is the ceremony?

About an hour with Mass, forty minutes without.

item.title: Mass Intentions
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Since the earliest centuries Catholics have asked that a Mass be offered for a particular person or need. The whole Mass is prayed for that intention and the name is read aloud during the prayers of the faithful. It is one of the most loving things you can do for someone who has died, and a beautiful way to mark an anniversary, a recovery or a birthday.

How it works

  1. Choose the kind of intention

    Announced Masses have the name read at that Mass and printed in the bulletin; there is one intention per Mass, so popular dates go quickly. Unannounced intentions are offered by a priest at a Mass without a public intention, usually within the month, and can be requested at any time.

  2. Pick a date

    Weekday Masses are usually available two to three months ahead; Sunday Masses and anniversaries book up to a year ahead. The office keeps the book and will offer the nearest free date.

  3. Make the offering

    The customary offering in the Archdiocese of Toronto is $10 per Mass. It is not a fee — no one is ever refused for lack of means — but a way of sharing in the support of the priest and parish. Pay at the office, by envelope marked "Mass intention", or by e-transfer to giving@stcolumbatoronto.ca with the intention in the message.

  4. Receive a Mass card

    If the Mass is for someone else's loved one, the office can give you a card to send to the family confirming the date.

Sanctuary lamp and memorial candles

The sanctuary lamp that burns beside the tabernacle may be offered for an intention for one week (suggested offering $25), and the two large candles at the shrine of Our Lady for one month ($40). Intentions are listed in the bulletin.

Request a Mass intention

This intention is for

The office confirms the date by phone or email within two business days. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Thank you. Your request has been sent to the parish office, which will confirm the date with you.

Questions

Can a Mass be offered for someone who is not Catholic?

Yes. A Mass may be offered for any person, living or deceased, of any faith or none.

Can I request several Masses at once?

Yes — many families request a Mass on the anniversary of death each year, or a series of Masses. If we cannot accommodate all of them, the extra intentions are sent, with the offerings, to missionary priests who have few of their own.

Will the name be printed?

Announced intentions appear in the weekly bulletin. If you prefer privacy, ask for the intention to be listed as "special intention".

Questions? Call the office at 416-555-0142 or email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

Our Director of Music, Claire Dubois, leads a ministry of about seventy volunteers across four choirs and a team of cantors and instrumentalists. Joining

Come to any rehearsal, or email music@stcolumbatoronto.ca. New members sit with an experienced singer for their first month. Reading music helps but is not required; rehearsal recordings are shared so you can practise at home. Join a choir

Yes — the music library, the sound desk and the livestream audio all need volunteers who are free on weekday evenings.

Do you accept donations toward the organ?

The Organ Fund pays for tuning and maintenance. Gifts may be made through the parish giving page, designated "Organ Fund".

item.title: New Here?
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Walking into an unfamiliar church can feel like arriving at a party where everyone else knows the steps. Nobody at St. Columba will ask you to prove anything, and nobody minds if you sit at the back and watch. This page answers the questions visitors ask most often.

What happens at Mass

A Sunday Mass lasts about an hour (the 11:00 AM Mass with choir runs a little longer). The order is the same in every Catholic church in the world, so once you have been here once you will recognize it anywhere. Here is the shape of it.

  1. Arrive and find a seat

    Doors open thirty minutes before Mass. An usher can hand you a hymn book and a bulletin. Any empty seat is yours.

  2. Introductory rites

    We stand and sing as the priest and servers enter. There is a short prayer asking God's mercy and, on most Sundays, the Gloria.

  3. Liturgy of the Word

    We sit for two readings from the Bible and a psalm, then stand for the Gospel. The priest or deacon gives a homily of about ten minutes, and then we stand to say the Creed and pray for the world.

  4. Liturgy of the Eucharist

    Gifts of bread and wine are brought forward and the collection is taken. The priest prays the Eucharistic Prayer while we kneel. We stand to pray the Our Father and offer one another a sign of peace, usually a handshake or a nod.

  5. Holy Communion

    Catholics who have prepared come forward to receive. If you are not Catholic, or not ready, you are welcome to stay in your seat or to come forward with your arms crossed over your chest for a blessing.

  6. Sending forth

    Announcements, a final blessing and a closing hymn. The priest greets people at the door afterwards. Please say hello.

What should I wear?

Whatever you would wear to a friend's home for a meal; you will see suits and jeans. There is no charge, and the collection is voluntary.

Getting here

Parking

Our lot is behind the parish hall, with the entrance off Columba Avenue. It holds about sixty cars and fills up for the 11:00 AM Mass, so arrive early or plan on street parking. Columba Avenue and the side streets allow three-hour parking on Sundays; please respect the driveways of our neighbours. Four accessible spaces sit next to the east entrance.

TTC

Take Line 2 to Pape Station and walk north about eight minutes, or take the 25 Don Mills bus from the station to the stop at Columba Avenue, directly in front of the church. The 81 Thorncliffe Park bus also stops within two blocks.

Accessibility

The main doors on Columba Avenue have steps. The accessible entrance is on the east side of the church, with a push-button door and a ramp. Inside, the front pews on the left have cut-outs for wheelchairs and walkers. The church has a hearing loop; set your hearing aid to the T setting. An elevator connects the church level to the parish hall and the accessible washroom. Large-print hymn sheets are available from the ushers. Full details are on our accessibility page.

Families with children

Children belong at Mass, noise and all. If your little one needs a break, the cry room at the back left has a window, a speaker and a change table. During the 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM Masses from September to June, children aged four to nine are invited to Children's Liturgy of the Word: they leave after the opening prayer for a short reflection on the readings in the hall and return at the offertory. All leaders are screened under the Archdiocese's Safe Environment policy.

Washrooms, including a family washroom with a change table, are downstairs and beside the east entrance. See children and families for programs through the week.

Becoming a parishioner

You do not need to register to attend, but registering means we can issue tax receipts, send envelopes, and know who you are when you ask for a baptism, wedding or letter of reference. Fill in the online registration form, pick up a paper form at the back of the church, or phone 416-555-0142. A welcome package follows within two weeks.

Register with the parish
Mass times

Frequently asked questions

I am not Catholic. May I still come?

Yes. Everyone is welcome at Mass and at anything else we do. If you become curious about the faith itself, our Becoming Catholic page explains how adults explore it, with no commitment.

I have not been to church in years. Will anyone notice?

Only in the sense that we will be glad to see you. If you would like to talk to a priest about coming back, or to go to confession, see Reconciliation or phone the office for an appointment.

Which Mass should I choose?

Saturday 5:00 PM is quiet and quick. Sunday 9:00 AM draws many families with young children. The 11:00 AM has the full choir and is livestreamed. The 1:00 PM rotates between Spanish, Tagalog and Italian, and the 5:00 PM is led by young adults with contemporary music.

Is there coffee afterwards?

Yes, after the 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM Masses in the hall, hosted by the hospitality ministry. It is the easiest way to meet people.

Can I bring my service dog?

Yes. Service animals are welcome anywhere in the church and hall.

Still wondering about something? Email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca or ask an usher on Sunday. More answers are on our Questions & Answers page.

Short stories from parish life, posted every week or two. For dates and times, see the calendar; for this week's announcements, the bulletin.

Welcome Back Picnic this Sunday

September 14, 2026

The summer is over, the choir is back, and it is time to see everyone again. After the 11:00 AM Mass on Sunday, September 20, the front lawn becomes a picnic ground: burgers and veggie burgers from the Knights' grill, a bouncy castle, face painting, a bake table from the CWL and lawn games for all ages. Bring a chair or a blanket. Everything is free; donations go to the food pantry.

New to the parish? This is the easiest afternoon of the year to meet people. Look for the volunteers in green T-shirts — their job is to introduce you to someone.

Welcome, Fr. Joseph Nguyen

September 7, 2026

Fr. Joseph Nguyen joined us this month as associate pastor, following his ordination in May and a summer assignment downtown. Born in Mississauga to parents who arrived from Vietnam in 1985, he studied engineering at the University of Toronto before entering St. Augustine's Seminary. He will take a special interest in young adults, the Spanish-speaking community (he speaks Spanish well, having spent a pastoral year in Guatemala) and hospital visits. Fr. Joseph celebrates the Sunday 5:00 PM Mass most weeks; please introduce yourself.

ShareLife: a record year

September 1, 2026

Thanks to 412 donors, St. Columba raised $91,300 for ShareLife this year — 107 per cent of our goal and the most in the parish's history. Those gifts support Catholic Family Services, Covenant House, the Society of Sharing, refugee resettlement and the formation of seminarians, among more than forty agencies. Fr. Moreau will offer the 11:00 AM Mass on September 27 in thanksgiving for all who gave.

Hall elevator now in service

August 28, 2026

After two years of fundraising and four months of construction, the elevator connecting the church, the office and the parish hall is running. For the first time since the hall was built in 1968, every parish space is step-free. The project cost $284,000, including the new accessible washroom on the lower level; $220,000 came from parishioners' gifts to the Building Fund and the balance from an archdiocesan accessibility grant. A blessing of the elevator — and coffee in the hall afterwards — takes place after the 9:00 AM Mass on October 4. Thank you to everyone who gave, and to the Building Committee for a project delivered on time.

Forty teens, one weekend, no phones

August 18, 2026

Forty young people from EDGE and LIFE TEEN spent the weekend of August 14–16 at a retreat centre near Orangeville with Marcus Lee and eight adult leaders. The theme was "Called by Name"; the schedule included canoeing, a campfire Mass with Fr. Moreau, adoration under the stars and, memorably, a phone-free 48 hours. "I didn't think I'd survive," one Grade 10 participant wrote afterwards, "and then I didn't want to leave." Youth ministry resumes on Friday, September 18. Registration for the year is open on the youth ministry page.

Food pantry serves 90 families a week

August 5, 2026

Demand at the St. Vincent de Paul pantry has doubled in three years. Each Tuesday and Saturday morning, volunteers now pack groceries for about ninety households — seniors on fixed incomes, newcomer families and, increasingly, people who are working full time. The pantry's greatest needs are rice, cooking oil, canned fish, baby formula and diapers; the bins are at every church entrance, and financial gifts (which the Society uses to buy fresh food at wholesale prices) can be made through the giving page. The Thanksgiving food drive is October 10–11. How to help.

item.title: Our Faith
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The Catholic faith is two thousand years old and practised by more than a billion people, but it is not complicated at its heart. God made the world and loves it. In Jesus Christ, God became one of us, died for us and rose from the dead. The Holy Spirit gathers us into the Church, feeds us with the sacraments and sends us out to love our neighbours. Everything else we teach and do grows from that. This section of the website is for anyone who wants to understand it better, whether you have been Catholic all your life or are looking in from outside for the first time.

What Catholics believe

Catholics believe in one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. We believe that Jesus of Nazareth is truly God and truly human, that he founded the Church on the apostles, and that he is really present in the Eucharist we celebrate at every Mass. We believe that the Bible is the inspired word of God, read and understood within the living tradition of the Church. We believe that every human being, from conception to natural death, carries the image of God and deserves dignity, and that we will be judged on how we treated the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner.

We also believe that faith is not a private possession. It is meant to be lived in a community, celebrated in the sacraments, and shared. That is why a parish exists.

Growing in faith as an adult

Many Catholics stopped learning about their faith at Confirmation. The parish offers several ways to pick it up again. Sr. Agnes leads a Bible study on Wednesday mornings after the 8:30 Mass and a six-week adult formation series each Lent and Advent. The Alpha course, an informal ten-week exploration of the basics over dinner, runs every autumn. Formation for Discipleship, the Archdiocese's program for adults, offers online courses through the year. See faith formation for dates.

Have a question about the faith?

There is no such thing as a foolish question. Email Sr. Agnes Ibeh at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca or ext. 25, or speak with either priest after Mass. If your question is about coming back to the Church after time away, Fr. Moreau would be glad to meet you privately.

item.title: Outreach & Social Justice
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
"For I was hungry and you gave me food." Everything on this page is a parish's answer to that sentence. Most of it happens in the hall, on Saturday mornings, and in the homes of neighbours you will never read about — and every part of it needs hands.

Out of the Cold

Wednesday nights · November to March · parish hall

A hot supper, a warm bed and breakfast for up to 40 guests experiencing homelessness, in partnership with neighbouring churches and a downtown agency. Volunteer shifts: cooking (2–5 PM), supper and hospitality (5–9 PM), overnight (9 PM–7 AM, in pairs), breakfast and cleanup (6–8 AM).

Contact: Joan Petrie · ootc@stcolumbatoronto.ca

St. Vincent de Paul

Food pantry Tue & Sat 10–12 · home visits

Groceries for ninety households a week and practical help with rent, utilities and furniture.

St. Vincent de Paul

Refugee sponsorship

Committee · through ORAT

The parish has sponsored eleven families since 2015; the current family arrived from Eritrea in February.

Refugee sponsorship

Development and Peace — Caritas Canada

Lent campaign · Share Lent collection 5th Sunday of Lent

The Canadian Church's international development agency, supporting partners in the Global South. The parish group runs the Lenten campaign and a fall action.

Contact: Louise Tremblay · devp.org

ShareLife

Archdiocesan appeal · collections March, May, June

Funds Catholic Family Services, Covenant House, the Society of Sharing, Silent Voice and forty other agencies. Parish goal $85,000.

sharelife.org

Prison ministry

Monthly · Toronto East Detention Centre

Parishioners join the archdiocesan chaplaincy team for Sunday services and one-to-one visits; training and clearance required.

Chaplaincies

Seasonal drives

Thanksgiving · Christmas · back-to-school · Coats for Kids

Food, hampers, gifts for 120 children, school supplies and winter coats, with the Knights and CWL.

Dates

Advocacy

Justice & Peace committee · quarterly

Letters, deputations and education on housing, palliative care, migrants and the environment, guided by Catholic social teaching and the Archdiocese's public policy office.

Three ways to help

  • Time. A pantry morning, an Out of the Cold shift, a drive to a refugee family's medical appointment. Sign up on the volunteer page; most roles need only low-risk screening.
  • Money. Designate a gift on the giving page to St. Vincent de Paul, Out of the Cold or refugee sponsorship. Every dollar goes to the program.
  • Prayer. The petitions at every Mass name the poor, the homeless, refugees and prisoners; the prayer chain prays for our guests by first name.

Why the Church does this

Catholic social teaching rests on the dignity of every person, made in God's image; on the common good; on solidarity with the poor; and on care for creation. It is not a political program but a way of seeing. The parish's Justice & Peace committee offers a four-week introduction each autumn, and the Archdiocese's Office for Refugees and its social justice office provide resources for parish groups.

I have a criminal record. Can I volunteer?

Often, yes. Talk to the screening coordinator in confidence; many roles do not require a police check, and a record is not an automatic bar.

Can my company or school group volunteer as a team?

Yes — pantry sorting and Out of the Cold cooking work well for groups of six to ten. Email the office two weeks ahead.

item.title: Papal Blessings & Certificates
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Papal Blessings

A Papal Blessing is a hand-lettered parchment, bearing the Holy Father's image and signature of the Office of Papal Charities, granting the Apostolic Blessing to a person or couple on a special occasion: a wedding, a 25th, 50th or 60th anniversary, a milestone birthday, an ordination or religious profession, or a First Communion. It is a treasured gift for parents and grandparents.

  1. Allow time

    Parchments are prepared in Rome and take two to three months to arrive, so request at least four months before the date.

  2. Ask the parish for a letter

    The request must be accompanied by a letter from the pastor confirming the recipients are practising Catholics in good standing. Complete the form below or call the office; the letter is ready within a week.

  3. Submit the request to Rome

    Requests are made through the Office of Papal Charities (Elemosineria Apostolica) website, where you choose the parchment design, upload the pastor's letter and pay the offering (roughly €25–€60 depending on size, plus shipping). The parchment is mailed to you directly. The office can submit the request on your behalf if you prefer.

Sacramental certificates

Every baptism, confirmation and marriage celebrated at St. Columba is recorded permanently in the parish registers, and notations are added when a person is later confirmed, married or ordained. Certificates are needed for marriage, to be a godparent or sponsor, for Catholic school registration and for ordination or religious life. Certificates are free; please allow five business days. If the sacrament took place at another parish, request it from that parish — we can help you find the address.

Letters of good standing

Godparents and Confirmation sponsors need a letter from their own parish confirming they are confirmed, practising Catholics who, if married, were married in the Church. If St. Columba is your parish, request the letter below; we ask that you be registered and known to us for at least six months. If you are new, come and introduce yourself to one of the priests after Mass first.

Certificates are issued only to the person named, their parents (for minors) or another parish. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Thank you. The office will contact you when your document is ready.

Questions

The name on my baptism record is spelled differently from my legal name.

Registers record the name given at baptism. Bring your birth certificate; we can add a notation and the certificate will show both.

Can I get a copy of my parents' or grandparents' records?

Records of living people are released only to them. Records of the deceased, and records more than 100 years old, may be released to family for genealogy at the pastor's discretion.

I was baptized in a country where the parish no longer exists.

A sworn statement by a parent or the godparent who was present can substitute; the priest will help you prepare it.

item.title: Parish Councils
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Under Church law the pastor is responsible for the parish, but no pastor should carry that responsibility alone. Two councils and two committees, made up of parishioners who give their evenings for free, help Fr. Moreau read the needs of the community, spend its money wisely, keep the roof sound, and make sure people know what is going on. Their meetings are not secret. Minutes are posted on the bulletin board by the east entrance and summarized in the bulletin, and any parishioner can bring an item forward.

Parish Pastoral Council

The Pastoral Council is a consultative body that helps the pastor discern the direction of the parish. It does not run ministries or manage money; it listens, reflects and advises. Its main work over the past two years was the consultation that produced the 2025–2028 pastoral plan, and its main work now is helping the pastor keep that plan on track.

Members serve a three-year term, renewable once. Half are elected by parishioners at the annual parish meeting each May; half are appointed by the pastor so that every language community and age group has a voice.

Members by role

  • Chair — Grace Okafor, elected 2024
  • Vice-chair — Roberto Mendes, Portuguese community
  • Secretary — Jennifer Tan
  • Ex officio — Rev. Daniel Moreau (pastor), Rev. Joseph Nguyen, Deacon Paul Ferreira, Sr. Agnes Ibeh
  • Elected members — one representative each for liturgy, faith formation, outreach and social justice, youth and young adults
  • Appointed members — one representative each for the Spanish, Tagalog, Italian and Tamil communities, plus one for seniors

Meetings and raising an item

The council meets on the second Tuesday of the month, 7:30–9:00 PM, in the rectory meeting room, September through June. To raise an item, email the secretary at office@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "Pastoral Council" in the subject line at least one week before the meeting, or put a note in the suggestion box at the back of the church. You will get a written reply after the meeting, usually within two weeks.

Finance Council

Every parish in the Archdiocese of Toronto is required to have a Finance Council. Ours reviews the monthly accounts, prepares the annual budget, approves any spending over $5,000, oversees the annual review by the Archdiocese, and reports to parishioners each February. Members are appointed by the pastor for three-year terms and bring accounting, banking, legal and property experience. The current chair is Anthony Carvalho, CPA; the council meets on the third Wednesday of the month at 7:00 PM.

2025 financial summary

These figures are from the report presented at the February 2026 parish meeting. The full report, with notes, is available from the office.

Separately, parishioners gave $96,800 to ShareLife in 2025, exceeding our parish goal of $90,000. ShareLife funds are collected by the parish but passed entirely to the Archdiocese's charitable agencies and are not part of parish income. To support the parish, see ways to give.

Building & Maintenance Committee

A subcommittee of the Finance Council, this group of six parishioners with trades and engineering backgrounds walks the buildings twice a year, keeps a ten-year capital plan, gets quotes for major work and supervises contractors. Current priorities are the church roof (replacement scheduled for summer 2027), the hall kitchen, and converting the remaining lighting to LED. Chair: Frank Petrucci. Meets quarterly, or as projects require. Parishioners who notice a problem with the buildings should tell the office; the committee reviews every report.

Communications Committee

Formed in 2023, the Communications Committee looks after the weekly bulletin, this website, the parish email list, the livestream and the sign on Columba Avenue. It also helps ministries publicize their events and makes sure notices reach every language community. Members include a retired journalist, a graphic designer, two high-school students who run the livestream and the parish secretary. Chair: Priya Raman. Meets on the first Monday of the month at 7:00 PM. To submit a bulletin notice, email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca by Tuesday noon for the following weekend.

Serving on a council

Vacancies are announced in the bulletin each spring. Any registered parishioner over eighteen may stand for the Pastoral Council; the Finance Council seeks people with relevant professional experience. All members complete the Archdiocese's volunteer screening. If you would like to know more, speak with any council member after Mass or contact the office.

item.title: Parish School
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Toronto is one of the few places in the world where publicly funded Catholic schools sit at the heart of parish life. St. Columba Catholic School, part of the Toronto Catholic District School Board (TCDSB), opened in 1958 on Columba Avenue, just two blocks north of the church, and serves about 380 students from Junior Kindergarten to Grade 8. The parish and the school are separate institutions with one mission: to help children know Christ and grow into good, capable, generous people.

Sacramental preparation

In the Archdiocese of Toronto, the parish, not the school, prepares children for the sacraments, and families register through the parish. The school supports that preparation in religion class, where the Grade 2 curriculum covers Reconciliation and First Communion and the Grade 7 curriculum covers Confirmation. Sr. Agnes, our Catechetical Coordinator, meets the school's Grade 2 and Grade 7 teachers each September to align what is taught in class with what happens in the parish program. Children who attend other schools, including public schools, are equally welcome in our sacramental programs; see Sacramental Preparation.

How school and parish work together

  • School Masses. The whole school comes to the church for Mass at the opening of the year in September, on All Saints, in Advent, on Ash Wednesday, in Easter season and for the Grade 8 graduation Mass in June. Fr. Nguyen also celebrates a monthly Mass in the school gym for one division at a time. Parents are always welcome.
  • Chaplaincy. Fr. Nguyen serves as the school's parish priest liaison, visiting classrooms, leading Advent and Lent reconciliation services for Grades 3 to 8, and being available to families and staff. The school also has a TCDSB chaplaincy lead on staff who coordinates retreats and prayer life.
  • Catholic School Council. A parish representative, appointed by the pastor, sits on the school council; currently that is Deacon Ferreira.
  • Shared outreach. Students run a Lenten food drive for our St. Vincent de Paul conference, sing at the parish Christmas concert, and serve at the Sunday 9:00 AM Mass as altar servers and readers.
  • Youth ministry. Marcus Lee visits the Grade 7 and 8 classes each fall to invite students to the parish youth group, which is the bridge from elementary school to high school faith life.

Pastor's letter for school registration

Some TCDSB schools ask for proof of Catholic baptism at registration. If you need a baptismal certificate, or a letter from the pastor confirming that your family is registered with the parish, contact the office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. Certificates take about a week; letters can usually be done in a day or two.

Registering at St. Columba Catholic School

Registration is handled by the school and the TCDSB, not the parish. Kindergarten registration for the following September opens each January, and families may register at any time during the year if they move into the area. To register a child you will generally need proof of the child's age (birth certificate or passport), proof of address, immunisation records, and, for Catholic admission, the child's or a parent's Catholic baptismal certificate. Contact the school office directly, or start online through the Board's website.

tcdsb.org

Catholic high schools

Graduates of St. Columba Catholic School go on to TCDSB secondary schools across the east end of the city, including the Catholic high schools closest to East York and the Board's specialty programs in the arts, technology and French immersion. Open houses take place in October and November, and Grade 8 families receive information from the school in the fall. Our parish youth group and 5:00 PM Sunday Mass are where many of our teens stay connected to the parish after they scatter to different high schools; see Youth Ministry.

Rosary Apostolate in the schools

Once a month from October to May, volunteers from the Rosary Apostolate visit every classroom at St. Columba Catholic School to pray a decade of the rosary with the children and teach them about the mysteries and the life of Mary. The Apostolate is a lay movement active across the Archdiocese; our parish team has nine members and is led by Concetta Bruno (rosary@stcolumbatoronto.ca). Volunteers complete high-risk screening and a short training session in September. It is a wonderful ministry for retirees and for parents with a free weekday morning.

Frequently asked

My child attends a public school. Can they still make First Communion here?

Yes. Sacramental preparation happens through the parish, and about a quarter of the children in our programs attend public or private schools. Register in September through the parish office.

Do we have to be parishioners to attend the school?

No. Admission is set by the TCDSB. But families who worship here find the connection between school and parish much richer, and registering with the parish is simple; see Register with the Parish.

Does the school have before- and after-school care?

Ask the school office; child-care programs in TCDSB schools are run by licensed providers and change from year to year.

Can our family attend the school Masses?

Always. They are announced in the bulletin and on the school's newsletter, and there is room at the back of the church.

Questions about the parish's work with the school? Contact Sr. Agnes Ibeh at 416-555-0142 ext. 25 or faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

item.title: Pastoral Plan
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
In the autumn of 2024, as the parish marked its seventieth anniversary, the Pastoral Council asked a simple question: what should St. Columba look like at seventy-five? More than four hundred parishioners answered, through listening sessions in six languages, a survey, and conversations after every Mass for two months. This plan is what we heard, distilled into five priorities. It was approved by Fr. Moreau and the Pastoral Council in January 2025 and covers three years. Each priority has three goals and a measure so that the parish can see, honestly, whether it is getting there.

Our vision

“By 2028, St. Columba will be a parish where every person who walks through the door is known by name, formed in the faith, and sent out to serve East York in the love of Christ.”

Vision statement, Pastoral Plan 2025–2028

Five priorities

What we will do

The order below is not a ranking. Worship comes first because everything else flows from the altar.

1. Worship: celebrate the liturgy with reverence and joy

  • Train and commission 40 new liturgical ministers (lectors, extraordinary ministers of Communion, ushers, servers) by June 2026, so that no ministry depends on the same twelve people.
  • Establish a second choir for the 9:00 AM Mass by Advent 2026, and grow the youth choir to 25 singers.
  • Add a monthly Mass in Tamil by 2027 and provide printed worship aids in all six languages for Christmas and Easter.

Measure: the number of active liturgical ministers in the parish database, reported to the Pastoral Council each June, and the October count of Mass attendance required by the Archdiocese.

2. Formation: help every age grow in faith

  • Offer at least one adult formation series every Advent and Lent and run the Alpha course every autumn, with a goal of 120 adults participating each year.
  • Re-launch the parish's sacramental preparation for First Communion and Confirmation with a family-based model by September 2026, so that parents are formed alongside their children.
  • Ensure every catechist and youth leader completes the Archdiocese's Formation for Discipleship foundations course by 2027.

Measure: annual participation counts for adult programs; percentage of catechists with completed formation, reported by Sr. Agnes each September.

3. Community: know one another by name

  • Build a team of welcomers so that a greeter is at every door at every weekend Mass, and every newly registered family receives a personal visit or call within a month.
  • Hold one parish-wide social event each season that brings the language communities together, beginning with a multicultural food festival in June 2025.
  • Launch a seniors' outreach so that every homebound parishioner is visited at least monthly and receives Communion if they wish.

Measure: new registrations per year and the share contacted within 30 days; the number of homebound parishioners on the visiting list and visits logged.

4. Outreach: serve East York

  • Expand the St. Vincent de Paul food cupboard to open twice a week and increase households served from 40 to 60 a month by 2027.
  • Sponsor one refugee family through the Office for Refugees of the Archdiocese of Toronto in each year of the plan.
  • Partner with the two parish schools and a local seniors' residence on a yearly service project involving the youth group.

Measure: households served and food distributed, from the St. Vincent de Paul conference's annual report; refugee families welcomed; youth service hours logged.

5. Stewardship: care for what we have been given

  • Increase the share of households giving through Pre-Authorized Giving from 22 per cent to 40 per cent by 2028, so that parish income is stable through the summer and winter.
  • Complete the church roof replacement in 2027 from the capital reserve without a special campaign, and convert all lighting to LED.
  • Publish a plain-language financial report every February and post Pastoral and Finance Council minutes within two weeks of each meeting.

Measure: PAG participation rate and capital reserve balance, from the Finance Council's annual report; minutes posted on time.

How you can help

Give an hour a month

Most of the goals above need people more than money. Welcomers, lectors, drivers for seniors, food cupboard volunteers and catechists are the plan's engine.

Volunteer

Sign up for PAG

Pre-Authorized Giving takes five minutes to set up and means the parish can plan. You choose the amount; you can change it any time.

Ways to give

Come to a formation series

The plan will only work if parishioners keep learning. Join Alpha this autumn or the Lenten series, and bring a neighbour.

Faith formation

Keeping ourselves honest

The Pastoral Council reviews progress on every goal each June and reports at the annual parish meeting, where any parishioner may ask questions. A one-page scorecard appears in the bulletin every September. Goals that are not working will be changed rather than quietly forgotten. Questions or suggestions may go to any council member or to office@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "Pastoral Plan" in the subject line. See parish councils for how the council works.

Read the full plan

The complete document runs to twelve pages, with the consultation findings, the theology behind each priority, and the full list of measures. Printed copies are available at the back of the church.

Every week the parish prays for people it has never met: a neighbour's father in hospital, a student writing exams, a marriage under strain, a family grieving. Requests reach us through this page, the office and the prayer box at the back of the church, and they are prayed for in three ways.

Same day

Prayer chain

Sixty parishioners receive requests by email and pray for them that day. First names only are shared.

Sunday

Prayers of the faithful

With your permission, the intention is included in the petitions at all weekend Masses.

In person

A visit

If you would like someone to pray with you at home or in hospital, a priest or a Legion of Mary member will come.

Anointing & visits

Send a prayer request

Requests are read only by the pastor and the prayer chain coordinator. See our privacy policy. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Thank you. Your request has been received and will be prayed for today.

A prayer for the sick

Lord Jesus, you went about doing good and healing all who were ill. Be near to those we name before you today. Give them strength in weakness, peace in fear, and the company of people who love them. Bless the hands of those who care for them. Let none of them feel alone, and bring them to healing of body and soul. Amen.

What happens to your request

Requests sent through this page go to the pastor and the prayer chain coordinator, Maureen Kelly, and to no one else. Within a few hours the intention is passed to the chain, using a first name only. If you ticked the box, it is added to the petitions read at the weekend Masses ("for Maria, who is seriously ill"). If you asked for a visit, Fr. Moreau, Fr. Nguyen or a screened pastoral visitor will phone you within two days to arrange a time. Requests are kept for one month and then deleted; nothing is published online.

You may also drop a written request in the wooden prayer box at the back of the church, or phone the office. Requests for someone who is dying should always come by phone — day or night at 416-555-0142, option 9 — so that a priest can come for the Anointing of the Sick.

Join the prayer chain

If you can commit to praying for the requests that arrive each day — it takes a few minutes — email prayerchain@stcolumbatoronto.ca. Members are asked to keep every request confidential. Those who are homebound are especially welcome; many of our most faithful intercessors pray from their kitchen tables.

item.title: Prayers
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Prayer is talking with God and letting God talk with you. It can be done in your own words at the kitchen sink, and with words the Church has prayed for centuries. The prayers below are the ones you will hear at Mass, at a bedside, at a graveside and in the pews when the Rosary is said. Click any prayer to open its text.

Common prayers

The Sign of the Cross

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Forehead, chest, left shoulder, right shoulder. It begins and ends almost every Catholic prayer.

The Our Father (the Lord's Prayer)

Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.

The Hail Mary

Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen.

The Glory Be

Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

The Apostles' Creed

I believe in God, the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Amen.

Act of Contrition

O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended thee, and I detest all my sins because of thy just punishments, but most of all because they offend thee, my God, who art all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of thy grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasions of sin. Amen.

Said in the confessional. See Reconciliation.

Hail, Holy Queen (Salve Regina)

Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve; to thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. Turn, then, most gracious advocate, thine eyes of mercy toward us, and after this our exile show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. Pray for us, O holy Mother of God, that we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ. Amen.

Prayer to St. Michael the Archangel

St. Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle. Be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil. May God rebuke him, we humbly pray; and do thou, O Prince of the heavenly host, by the power of God, cast into hell Satan and all the evil spirits who prowl about the world seeking the ruin of souls. Amen.

Grace before meals

Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

After meals: We give thee thanks, almighty God, for all thy benefits, who livest and reignest for ever and ever. Amen.

Parish prayer to St. Columba

St. Columba, who left the shore of your own country to carry the light of Christ to a people not your own, pray for this parish of travellers and their children. Teach us to make a home for the stranger, to keep the faith in a new land, and to sail wherever the Lord sends us without fear. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

Written for the parish's 70th anniversary and prayed at the end of the Prayer of the Faithful on our patronal feast, June 9.

How to pray the Rosary

The Rosary is a meditation on twenty scenes, called mysteries, from the lives of Jesus and Mary, prayed on a string of beads. It takes about twenty minutes and is prayed in the church every weekday after the 8:30 AM Mass; anyone may join, and spare rosaries are in the basket by the Mary altar.

  1. Begin

    Holding the crucifix, make the Sign of the Cross and pray the Apostles' Creed. On the first bead pray an Our Father; on the next three, a Hail Mary each (for faith, hope and love); then a Glory Be.

  2. Announce the first mystery

    Say the name of the mystery (for example, "the first Joyful Mystery, the Annunciation") and picture the scene for a moment. Pray an Our Father on the large bead.

  3. Pray the decade

    Pray a Hail Mary on each of the ten small beads while keeping the mystery in mind, then a Glory Be. Many add the short Fátima prayer.

  4. Repeat for five mysteries

    Announce the next mystery, Our Father, ten Hail Marys, Glory Be, and so on around the beads.

  5. Finish

    Pray the Hail, Holy Queen, then the Sign of the Cross.

The mysteries by day of the week

During Advent and Christmas the Joyful Mysteries are often prayed on Sundays, and during Lent the Sorrowful.

The Divine Mercy Chaplet

The Chaplet is prayed on rosary beads and takes about seven minutes. It is prayed in our parish at 3:00 PM on Fridays in Lent and on Divine Mercy Sunday, the Sunday after Easter. Its shape:

  • Begin with the Sign of the Cross, an Our Father, a Hail Mary and the Apostles' Creed.
  • On each large bead: "Eternal Father, I offer you the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of your dearly beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in atonement for our sins and those of the whole world."
  • On each of the ten small beads: "For the sake of his sorrowful Passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world."
  • After five decades, three times: "Holy God, Holy Mighty One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us and on the whole world."

Prayer in the parish

Rosary weekdays after the 8:30 AM Mass · Novena to Our Lady of Perpetual Help Wednesdays 7:30 PM · Adoration Thursdays 9:00 AM–12:00 PM and First Fridays 7:00–8:00 PM. To ask the parish to pray for someone, use the prayer request form; to have a Mass offered, see Mass intentions. More on devotions and Adoration.

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
St. Columba Parish collects personal information only when we need it to serve you: to register your family, to prepare your child for a sacrament, to issue a tax receipt, or to answer a message you send us. We treat that information as a trust. This policy explains what we collect through this website and in the parish office, how it is used and protected, and what you can ask of us. It follows the privacy guidelines of the Archdiocese of Toronto and the principles of Canada's federal privacy law. Last updated September 2026.

What we collect and why

We do not sell, rent or trade personal information, and we do not send marketing on behalf of anyone else. We share information outside the parish only with the Archdiocese of Toronto where policy requires it (for example sacramental records and volunteer screening), with the service providers named below, and where the law requires.

Sacramental records

Records of baptisms, confirmations, marriages and deaths are kept permanently in bound registers, as canon law requires, and a copy is held by the Archdiocesan Archives. They are not public. A certificate is issued to the person the record concerns (or a parent or guardian for a minor), or to another parish preparing that person for a sacrament. Notations of confirmation, marriage and holy orders are added to the baptismal record over a person's lifetime. Records of adopted persons and other sensitive entries are handled under archdiocesan rules and released only with the Chancery's approval. To request a certificate, contact the office with your full name, date of birth and the approximate date of the sacrament; there is no fee, and most certificates are ready within a week.

How long we keep information

  • Website messages: deleted from the form service within 90 days once handled; the office may keep the email thread for one year.
  • Parish registration: for as long as you are registered, and for two years after you tell us you have moved.
  • Donation records: seven years after the end of the year of the gift, as required by the Canada Revenue Agency.
  • Volunteer screening files: while you volunteer and for seven years afterwards.
  • Sacramental registers: permanently.

Third-party services

This website relies on a few outside services. Each processes only the information needed for its job and is bound by its own privacy policy.

  • Form handling. Website forms are delivered to the parish office by the form service of our website host (Netlify Forms on the demonstration site; the built-in Form block when the site is hosted on WordPress.com). Submissions are stored on the host's servers until the office downloads and deletes them.
  • Google Calendar and Google Maps. The calendar on our Events page and the map on our contact page are embedded from Google, which may set its own cookies within the embed.
  • YouTube. Mass livestreams and archived videos are embedded from YouTube using its privacy-enhanced mode, which does not set tracking cookies until you press play.
  • Online giving. Online donations are made through the Archdiocese of Toronto's secure portal. The parish never sees or stores your card number.

Cookies

This site sets no cookies of its own and uses no advertising or analytics trackers. Embedded services (YouTube, Google Calendar, Google Maps) may set cookies when you interact with them; you can block these in your browser without losing access to the rest of the site.

Security

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in the parish office with access limited to the pastor and office staff. Electronic records live on password-protected parish computers and the Archdiocese's parish database, never on personal devices, and website traffic is encrypted.

Your rights: access and correction

  1. Ask

    Write to the parish office (email or letter) asking to see the personal information we hold about you, or to correct it. Tell us which records you mean if you can.

  2. We confirm your identity

    We will ask for identification, or for a parent or guardian's consent where a minor's records are involved, before releasing anything.

  3. We respond within 30 days

    You will receive a copy of your information, or an explanation if part of it cannot be released (for example, references given in confidence, or another person's information mixed with yours). Corrections to sacramental registers follow canon law and may require documentary proof.

You may also ask us to stop contacting you or to remove you from the parish roll; we will do so unless a legal or canonical retention rule applies.

Photographs and changes to this policy

Identifiable photos of children taken at parish events require a parent's written consent, and we will remove any photograph of you or your child from the website on request. Changes to this policy are posted here with a new "last updated" date.

Questions or concerns about privacy? Contact Teresa Alvarez, Office Manager and privacy contact, at 416-555-0142 ext. 21 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca, or write to St. Columba Parish, 1240 Columba Avenue, Toronto, ON M4K 2R6. If you are not satisfied with our response, you may raise the matter with the Archdiocese of Toronto through archtoronto.org.
