item.title: Questions & Answers
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The parish office answers the same twenty questions several times a week, and is always glad to. But if it is nine o'clock at night and you just want to know whether you can get a baptism certificate by email, this page is for you. Click a question to open the answer.

Visiting

When are Masses, and do I need to arrive early?

Saturday 5:00 PM; Sunday 9:00, 11:00 AM, 1:00 PM (Spanish, Tagalog or Italian by the week) and 5:00 PM; weekdays 8:30 AM. Ten minutes early is plenty, except at Christmas and Easter. Full schedule on Mass times.

I am not Catholic. Can I attend, and can I receive Communion?

You are welcome at every Mass. Holy Communion is reserved for Catholics who have made their First Communion, because it expresses full unity with the Church; you are invited to come forward with your arms crossed for a blessing instead. See New here?.

Is the church accessible?

Yes. The east-side entrance has a ramp and automatic door, there is an elevator to the hall, an accessible washroom, wheelchair spaces in the front pews, and a hearing loop. Details are on the accessibility page.

Is Mass available online?

The 11:00 AM Sunday Mass is livestreamed and the recording stays online for a week. See livestream. If you cannot come to Mass because of illness, please tell the office; a minister can bring Communion to your home.

When can I go to confession?

Saturday 3:30–4:30 PM and Wednesday 6:15–6:45 PM in the confessional at the back of the church, or by appointment with either priest. See Reconciliation.

Sacraments

How do I have my baby baptized?

Register with the parish, then call the office to book a date. Parents attend one preparation evening with Deacon Paul. Baptisms are usually on the second and fourth Sundays at 2:30 PM. No fee; a donation is welcome. You will need the child's birth certificate and at least one godparent who is a confirmed, practising Catholic. See Baptism.

When do children make First Communion and Confirmation?

First Communion is normally in Grade 2 and Confirmation in Grade 7, with preparation running from October to the spring. Registration opens each September through Sr. Agnes at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca. Children in Catholic schools still register through the parish. See sacramental preparation.

We want to get married here. How far ahead should we call?

Contact Fr. Moreau at least twelve months before your hoped-for date. A marriage preparation course is required, and there is paperwork to gather, especially if either of you was baptized elsewhere or married before. The suggested church offering is $500, including the organist. See Marriage.

How do I arrange a funeral?

Call the office at any hour; outside office hours choose option 9 to reach a priest. We will coordinate dates with your funeral home and meet with you to plan the readings and music. Catholic Cemeteries & Funeral Services of the Archdiocese can help with burial: catholic-cemeteries.ca. See Funerals and bereavement ministry.

I am an adult who was never baptized, or never confirmed. What do I do?

Join OCIA, the process by which adults become Catholic or complete their sacraments. It meets Tuesdays at 7:00 PM from September to Easter, and there is no obligation in coming to find out more. See Becoming Catholic.

Getting involved

How do I join a ministry or volunteer?

Browse the ministry directory and contact the coordinator listed, or fill in the volunteer form and we will match you. Every volunteer completes the Archdiocese's screening, which for most ministries is a short form and an information session; ministries involving children, youth or vulnerable adults also require a police check. See volunteer screening.

Can I sing in the choir if I cannot read music?

Yes. The parish choir rehearses Thursdays at 7:30 PM and welcomes anyone who can hold a tune; parts are taught by ear as well as from the score. Contact Claire Dubois at music@stcolumbatoronto.ca. See music ministry.

Is there something for teenagers and young adults?

The youth group for Grades 7–12 meets Friday evenings, and the young adult community (ages 18–35) gathers around the 5:00 PM Sunday Mass. Contact Marcus Lee at youth@stcolumbatoronto.ca. See youth ministry and young adults.

Practical

How do I get a baptism, confirmation or marriage certificate?

Email or phone the office with the full name, date of birth, approximate date of the sacrament and parents' names. Certificates are ready within five business days and can be picked up, mailed or scanned. Certificates for marriage must be freshly issued (within six months) and go directly to the receiving parish. No fee.

How do I donate, and will I get a tax receipt?

Give through the collection, offertory envelopes, Pre-Authorized Giving, e-transfer to giving@stcolumbatoronto.ca, or online through the Archdiocese's secure portal. Registered parishioners receive one tax receipt each February for the previous year's gifts of $20 or more. See ways to give.

Can I rent the parish hall?

Yes, for receptions, anniversaries, memorial lunches and community meetings. The hall seats 220, has a licensed kitchen and an elevator, and rents for a suggested $350 per evening for parishioners. Bookings are through Teresa Alvarez at ext. 21. See hall rentals.

How do I request a Mass for someone?

Ask at the office or use the Mass intention form. The suggested offering is $10. Weekend Masses are booked several months ahead; weekday Masses are usually available within a few weeks.

Where do I report a concern about a priest, staff member or volunteer?

Concerns about the safety of children or vulnerable adults should go to the police and the Archdiocese of Toronto. Our reporting misconduct page lists every contact and explains the Safe Environment policy.

Did not find your answer?

Phone the office Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM–4:00 PM (closed 12–1) at 416-555-0142, email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca, or use the contact form. We reply within two business days.

item.title: Reconciliation (Confession)
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The Sacrament of Reconciliation is where we hand over what we regret and receive God's forgiveness, spoken out loud by the priest. It takes five minutes. Nothing you say can ever be repeated by the priest, under any circumstances.

Regular times

  • 3:30 – 4:30 PMSat
  • 6:15 – 6:45 PMWed
  • 7:00 – 7:45 PMduring Adoration1st Fri

By appointment

  • Call 416-555-0142Office
  • Ask a priest after any Mass
  • Home or hospital visitfor the sick

Penitential services

  • Adventmid-DecemberSun 3 PM
  • LentMonday of Holy Week7 PM
  • Several priests available

How to go to confession

  1. Prepare

    Spend a few minutes in the church thinking honestly about your life since your last confession. The examination of conscience below can help.

  2. Begin

    Enter the confessional — you may kneel behind the screen or sit face to face. Say: "Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been (however long) since my last confession." If you have forgotten how it goes, say so; the priest will guide you.

  3. Confess

    Name your sins simply and honestly. You do not need to explain or excuse them. If unsure whether something is a sin, ask.

  4. Listen

    The priest may offer a word of advice, then gives a penance — usually a prayer or a small act of kindness.

  5. Act of Contrition

    Pray the Act of Contrition (below). The priest then says the prayer of absolution: "…I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Answer "Amen."

  6. Go in peace

    Do your penance soon, and thank God. That is all.

O my God, I am sorry for my sins with all my heart. In choosing to do wrong and failing to do good, I have sinned against you whom I should love above all things. I firmly intend, with your help, to do penance, to sin no more, and to avoid whatever leads me to sin. Our Saviour Jesus Christ suffered and died for us. In his name, my God, have mercy. Amen.

Act of Contrition

Examination of conscience

For adults
  • Has God been first in my life, or have I let work, money, comfort or fear take his place? Have I prayed?
  • Have I kept Sunday holy? Have I missed Mass through my own fault?
  • Have I used God's name carelessly, or spoken of my faith with contempt?
  • Have I honoured my parents and cared for my family? Have I been patient with my children, faithful to my spouse, present to my ageing parents?
  • Have I harmed anyone — by anger, violence, contempt, gossip, prejudice, or neglect of someone in need?
  • Have I been faithful and chaste in thought and action, according to my state in life?
  • Have I been honest — in my work, my taxes, my promises? Have I taken what was not mine?
  • Have I told the truth, kept confidences, and refused to damage another's reputation?
  • Have I been envious, or greedy, or ungrateful for what I have?
  • What good have I left undone that I could have done?
For young people
  • Do I talk to God, or only when I need something?
  • Do I go to Mass willingly, or make it a fight?
  • How do I treat my parents, brothers and sisters? Do I help at home?
  • Am I kind to people at school who are left out? Have I bullied, mocked or excluded anyone, in person or online?
  • Am I honest — about homework, about where I've been, about what I've done?
  • Do I treat my body and other people's bodies with respect? What do I look at online?
  • Have I taken things that aren't mine, or damaged things on purpose?
  • Do I say sorry and forgive when someone hurts me?

Questions

It has been twenty years. Where do I start?

Start by coming. Tell the priest it has been a long time and he will walk you through every step. Priests are always glad — not shocked — when someone returns.

Do I have to confess to a priest I know?

No. Both priests hear confessions, the screen is always available, and you may go to any parish. The seal of confession is absolute.

What if I forget a sin?

If you honestly forgot, it is forgiven with the rest. Mention it next time if it still troubles you.

Can children go to confession?

Children make their First Reconciliation in Grade 2, before First Communion, and are encouraged to come at the regular times with their parents afterwards. See First Reconciliation & Communion.

All sacraments

item.title: Refugee Sponsorship (ORAT)
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
"I was a stranger and you welcomed me." For more than forty years Catholics in Toronto have taken those words literally, sponsoring tens of thousands of refugees through their parishes. St. Columba has welcomed seven families since 2016, from Syria, Eritrea, Iraq and, most recently, Afghanistan. Our eighth sponsorship is underway. This page explains how the program works, what it asks of sponsors, and how you can be part of it.

What ORAT is

The Office for Refugees of the Archdiocese of Toronto (ORAT) is the archdiocesan agency that holds a Sponsorship Agreement with the Government of Canada. That agreement lets the Archdiocese act as a Sponsorship Agreement Holder, and it means that parishes, religious communities and groups of parishioners can sponsor refugees under its umbrella rather than forming their own private group from scratch. ORAT identifies refugees in need of resettlement, prepares and submits the immigration paperwork, trains parish groups, holds the sponsorship funds in trust, and supports groups through the whole year of settlement. Since it was founded, ORAT has helped bring several thousand refugees to safety in the Greater Toronto Area.

Learn more at orat.ca.

How a parish sponsorship works

  1. A group forms

    At least five parishioners, with the pastor's blessing, agree to form a sponsorship group. Our standing committee usually seeds each new group with two or three experienced members.

  2. The group chooses a case

    ORAT presents cases it has assessed: sometimes a family referred by the United Nations refugee agency, sometimes relatives of people already settled in Toronto ("family-linked" cases). The group commits to one.

  3. Funds are raised and held in trust

    The group raises the settlement budget, currently about $30,000 for a family of four, and deposits it with ORAT, which holds it in a dedicated trust account until arrival.

  4. ORAT files the application

    ORAT staff prepare the sponsorship undertaking and the refugees' application and submit them to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. Processing can take from a few months to two years or more, depending on the country.

  5. Training and preparation

    While the file is in process, the group completes ORAT's sponsor training, finds housing, gathers furniture and lines up a doctor, a school and a settlement agency.

  6. Arrival and the first year

    The group meets the family at Pearson, and for twelve months provides financial support, orientation and friendship until the family can stand on its own.

What sponsors commit to

Under the government agreement, sponsors are responsible for the newcomers for twelve months from the day they land (or until they become self-sufficient, if earlier). In practice that means:

  • Financial support at roughly the level of provincial social assistance: rent, food, clothing, transit and a start-up allowance for furniture and winter clothing.
  • Orientation: applying for health cards, social insurance numbers, bank accounts, child benefits and English classes; registering children in school; finding a family doctor and dentist.
  • Accompaniment: showing the family the neighbourhood, the transit system, the grocery stores and the parish; helping adults look for work; being there when the paperwork or the winter gets overwhelming.
  • Respect for the family's own faith and choices. Many families we sponsor are not Catholic, and no one is ever asked to attend church.

How much time does it take?

In the first month, expect two or three group members to be busy most days. After that, a typical volunteer gives two to four hours a week: a weekly visit, a ride to an appointment, help with a form. The commitment is shared across the whole group, so no one carries it alone.

Our sponsorship committee

The St. Columba Refugee Sponsorship Committee is a standing group of about twenty parishioners, drawn from our English, Spanish, Tagalog, Italian, Portuguese and Tamil communities, which is a real gift when a family arrives speaking a language one of us knows. The committee meets on the third Tuesday of the month at 7:30 PM in the parish hall meeting room, and reports to the pastor and the Parish Pastoral Council twice a year.

Coordinator: Nadia Haddad · refugees@stcolumbatoronto.ca · through the office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20.

How you can help

Give

Gifts to the sponsorship fund are tax-receipted. Use an offertory envelope marked "Refugee Sponsorship," send an e-transfer to giving@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "refugees" in the message, or give online through the archdiocesan portal and choose our parish. The current campaign for our eighth family stands at $22,400 of the $31,000 goal.

Join

New members are welcome at any committee meeting, and there is a role for everyone: drivers, tutors, people who know the health system, people who are handy with a furniture dolly, people who cook. All members complete volunteer screening, and those who will work directly with children complete a police vulnerable-sector check.

Donate goods

Before a family arrives, the committee publishes a specific list in the bulletin. Please do not drop off furniture or clothing unannounced; we have no storage, and the family's needs are particular.

Frequently asked

Can we sponsor relatives of a parishioner?

Often, yes. ORAT handles family-linked cases where a Toronto resident's relatives are recognised refugees abroad. Speak to Nadia and she will arrange an intake conversation with ORAT.

Where do the families live?

We try to house families within reach of the parish so that support is easy, but Toronto rents mean we sometimes look further east or north. The family chooses where to move after the first year.

What happens after the twelve months?

Formal responsibility ends, and friendship usually does not. Several of the families we sponsored years ago are now parishioners and committee members themselves.

Questions? Contact Nadia Haddad at refugees@stcolumbatoronto.ca or the parish office at 416-555-0142.

Visit orat.ca
Give
Outreach

item.title: Register with the Parish
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Whether you have just moved to East York, have been sitting in the same pew for years without ever filling in a form, or are returning to the Church after time away, we would love to have you registered. Registration is not a test and it costs nothing; it simply tells us who you are, how to reach you, and how we can serve your family. About 1,200 households are registered with St. Columba, and we hope yours will be next.

Why register

  • Sacraments. When you ask to have a child baptised, register for First Communion or Confirmation, or plan a wedding, the first question is whether you are registered. Having your details on file already saves a step.
  • Letters and certificates. Godparent and sponsor letters, and letters for Catholic school registration, can be issued only to registered, practising parishioners.
  • Tax receipts. Registration lets us track your offertory envelopes, pre-authorized giving and other gifts and issue one receipt each February.
  • Staying in touch. You receive the bulletin by email if you wish, notices about programs your family may be interested in, and a Christmas and Easter letter from the pastor.
  • Belonging. Registration is a way of saying "this is my parish." Ministries, councils and parish groups are built from the people on the roll.

Who can register

Anyone who worships regularly at St. Columba may register, whether or not you live within the parish boundaries; in the Archdiocese of Toronto, Catholics may belong to the parish where they actually pray. Households can be a single person, a couple, a family with children, or several generations under one roof. You do not need to be Catholic to register; spouses of other faiths, people in the OCIA process and friends of the parish are all welcome on the roll. Students home for the summer and newcomers to Canada should register too, even if they are not sure how long they will stay.

What happens after you register

  1. A welcome

    Within two weeks you will receive a welcome letter from Fr. Moreau, a copy of the current bulletin, and a card with the office contacts and Mass times.

  2. Envelopes, if you asked for them

    A box of numbered offertory envelopes is left for you at the office or in the vestibule rack under your name. New boxes are issued each December.

  3. Pre-authorized giving, if you are interested

    Teresa Alvarez will send you the PAG form and answer questions. Monthly gifts are withdrawn on the 1st or 15th; you can change or cancel any time.

  4. Your record

    Your household is entered in the parish database, which is used for envelopes, receipts and sacramental follow-up. See our Privacy Policy for how it is protected.

  5. Tax receipts

    One receipt for all your recorded gifts is mailed or emailed in February. Loose cash in the collection cannot be receipted, which is why envelopes matter.

Already registered? Keep us up to date

Moved, changed your phone number or email, welcomed a new baby, or lost a family member? Use the same form below and note "update" in the last field, or call the office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. If you have moved to another parish, let us know so we can close your envelope number and send your final receipt.

Register online

Your information is used only for parish records and is never shared or sold. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Welcome to St. Columba. Your registration has been received; look for a letter from Fr. Moreau within two weeks.

Prefer paper?

Print the registration form, fill it in, and drop it in the collection basket, through the office mail slot, or hand it to any usher. Forms are also in the rack at each entrance of the church.

Parish registration form (PDF)Download

Frequently asked

Is there a fee to register?

No. Registration is free, and there is no minimum donation.

I live in another parish's territory. Can I still register here?

Yes. Many parishioners come from across East York and beyond. If you later need something from your territorial parish, such as a permission for a wedding elsewhere, we will help you sort it out.

What if I have not been to church in a long time?

Then welcome back. Register, come to Mass, and if you would like to talk with a priest about picking things up again, say so on the form or see New Here.

Do I need to register before I can receive Communion?

No. Any Catholic in a state of grace may receive. Registration is about parish life and records, not about who is welcome at the altar.

Questions? Contact Ann Marie O'Connor, Parish Secretary, at 416-555-0142 ext. 20 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca. The office is open Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM (closed 12 to 1).

item.title: Report Misconduct
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Reporting abuse takes courage. Whether it happened last week or fifty years ago, whether it happened here or in another parish, whether you are the person harmed, a parent, or a witness, you will be believed, listened to and supported. This page sets out, as clearly as we can, every way to report, and what happens after you do. You do not have to choose the "right" channel; any of them will get help to you.

In an emergency

If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911. To report a crime that is not an emergency, call the Toronto Police Service non-emergency line at 416-808-2222. If you believe a child is being abused or neglected, Ontario law requires you to report it directly to a children's aid society; in Toronto, call the Children's Aid Society of Toronto at 416-924-4646 or the Catholic Children's Aid Society at 416-395-1500, at any hour. You do not need proof, and you do not need to tell the parish first.

Reporting to the Archdiocese of Toronto

Allegations of abuse or misconduct by any priest, deacon, religious, employee or volunteer serving in the Archdiocese are handled by the archdiocesan Safe Environment office under the Strengthening the Caring Community policy. You can contact that office directly, without going through the parish, through the contact details published at archtoronto.org. The office will:

  • Listen to you, in person, by phone or in writing, in the language you are most comfortable in;
  • Report any allegation involving a minor to the police and children's aid, and cooperate fully with their investigation;
  • Remove the accused person from ministry while the matter is examined;
  • Offer you counselling and pastoral support at the Archdiocese's expense, regardless of the outcome of any investigation;
  • Keep you informed of the process and its result.

Reporting to the parish

You may also report directly to the parish. Fr. Daniel Moreau, Pastor, can be reached at 416-555-0142 ext. 22 or pastor@stcolumbatoronto.ca. If the concern involves the pastor himself, contact the Archdiocese rather than the parish. Every report made to the parish about clergy, staff or volunteers is passed to the archdiocesan Safe Environment office the same day; the parish does not investigate on its own. Teresa Alvarez, our Safe Environment Coordinator (ext. 21), can also receive a report and will make sure it reaches the right people.

Reporting a bishop

Concerns about a bishop, including the Archbishop of Toronto, an auxiliary bishop or a retired bishop, whether for abuse or for mishandling a report of abuse, are handled by the Canadian Reporting System for Sexual Abuse or Cover-up by a Catholic Bishop, established by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops in response to Pope Francis's 2019 decree Vos estis lux mundi. Reports are received by an independent third-party service and forwarded to the appropriate Church authority, and may be made anonymously.

bishopreportingsystem.ca
Canadian bishops (CCCB)

What happens after you report

  1. You are heard

    A trained person meets with you or speaks with you by phone. You may bring a friend, family member or advocate. You will not be asked to confront the person you are reporting.

  2. Civil authorities are involved

    Any allegation involving a minor, or any allegation that may be a crime, is reported to police. The Church does not ask you to choose between a police report and a Church report; you may make both, and the Archdiocese will not obstruct or delay a criminal investigation.

  3. Protective measures

    The person named is placed on administrative leave or removed from their volunteer role while the matter is examined, whatever their position.

  4. Investigation

    Once any police process allows, the Archdiocese conducts its own review, which may involve an independent investigator and, for clergy, the archdiocesan review committee that includes lay experts. You will be told the outcome.

  5. Ongoing support

    Support for you does not end when the investigation does. Counselling, spiritual accompaniment and a pastoral response can continue for as long as they are helpful.

Support for victims and survivors

The Archdiocese of Toronto provides professional counselling to anyone who reports abuse by a person serving in the Church, and to their immediate family, without requiring a finding of fault first. If you would rather not approach the Church at all, that is understood; community services such as the Toronto Rape Crisis Centre, the Assaulted Women's Helpline (1-866-863-0511) and the Ontario Victim Support Line (1-888-579-2888) can help, and the parish will assist you in reaching them if you wish. Our clergy are available for pastoral conversation if you want it; no one is ever asked to forgive as a condition of being helped.

Confidentiality

Your report is shared only with the people who need to act on it: the Safe Environment office, the Archbishop or his delegate, the police and children's aid where required, and the accused person's superior. Your name is not shared with the wider parish, and it is not disclosed to the person accused without your knowledge. You may report anonymously, though this can limit what the Archdiocese is able to investigate. Records are kept securely and indefinitely so that a pattern can be recognised even years later.

No retaliation

Anyone who makes a report in good faith, or who cooperates with an investigation, is protected from retaliation of any kind: no loss of ministry, no exclusion from the parish, no pressure to withdraw. Retaliation is itself misconduct under archdiocesan policy and will be treated as such. Making a knowingly false report is also a serious matter, but an honest report that turns out to be mistaken is never held against the person who made it.

Concerns that are not about abuse, such as financial irregularities, harassment between adults or breaches of privacy, can be raised with the pastor, or with the Archdiocese if they involve the pastor, under the same principles of confidentiality and no retaliation.

If you are unsure whether what you experienced counts, or who to tell, contact the archdiocesan Safe Environment office or call the parish at 416-555-0142. Asking is always the right thing to do.

item.title: Safe Environment
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Parishes are full of trust. Parents hand their children to catechists, seniors open their doors to pastoral visitors, and young people confide in youth leaders. That trust is a gift, and protecting it is a duty. The Archdiocese of Toronto's Safe Environment policy, known as Strengthening the Caring Community, sets out what every parish must do to prevent abuse, to respond when concerns arise, and to build a culture in which everyone, especially the most vulnerable, is respected. St. Columba follows the policy in full. This page is a plain-language summary; the complete policy is published by the Archdiocese at archtoronto.org.

Our commitments

  • We screen every volunteer and employee before they begin, in proportion to the trust their role involves.
  • We train clergy, staff and volunteers to recognise abuse, maintain healthy boundaries and report concerns.
  • We follow a written code of conduct, and we expect every adult in ministry to sign it.
  • We report every allegation of abuse of a minor to the police and to the Archdiocese, without exception and without delay.
  • We support anyone who has been harmed, and we do not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises a concern in good faith.
  • We review our practices every year with the pastor, the Screening Committee and the Parish Pastoral Council.

Screening

All volunteers complete an application and an interview, and provide references. Those in "high-risk" ministries, meaning any role with unsupervised or regular access to children, youth, seniors or people with disabilities, also provide a police vulnerable-sector check and complete an orientation before they begin. Clergy and employees are screened by the Archdiocese as well as the parish. Screening is renewed on a set schedule, and the parish keeps confidential records of every step. For the full process see Volunteer Screening.

Training

Awareness training is required for every high-risk volunteer and for all staff and clergy, and is refreshed every three years. The session, about two hours, covers the kinds of abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, neglect and financial exploitation of vulnerable adults), the signs to watch for, the duty to report under Ontario's Child, Youth and Family Services Act, and how to respond if a child or adult discloses something to you. St. Columba offers the session in the parish hall three times a year, and the Archdiocese offers it online. Parents of children in our programs are welcome to attend.

Code of conduct for volunteers

Every volunteer in a high-risk ministry signs the archdiocesan code of conduct. Its main points are practical and easy to remember:

Alcohol is never served at youth events, and adults do not drink when responsible for minors. Overnight events require written parental consent, a minimum adult-to-youth ratio, and separate sleeping areas for adults and youth.

How concerns are handled

  1. Immediate danger: call 911

    If a child or adult is in immediate danger, call 911 first. Nothing in this policy delays that.

  2. Report

    Anyone who suspects a child is being abused has a legal duty in Ontario to report directly to a children's aid society. You do not need proof, and you do not need permission from the parish. Tell the pastor as well, unless the concern involves him, in which case contact the Archdiocese directly.

  3. The Archdiocese is notified

    The pastor reports every allegation involving clergy, staff or volunteers to the archdiocesan Safe Environment office the same day. The Archdiocese cooperates fully with police and children's aid.

  4. The person is stepped aside

    Anyone against whom an allegation is made is removed from ministry while the matter is investigated. This is a protective measure, not a judgment.

  5. Support and follow-up

    The person harmed and their family are offered pastoral and professional support. The parish community is informed in a way that protects privacy and prevents rumour.

Reporting misconduct

For the full list of ways to report abuse or misconduct, including the channels for reporting a bishop, see Report Misconduct. You may also contact the Archdiocese of Toronto's Safe Environment office directly at any time.

Who is responsible at St. Columba

  • Pastor: Rev. Daniel Moreau, ext. 22, is accountable for the policy in the parish.
  • Safe Environment Coordinator: Teresa Alvarez, Office Manager, ext. 21, keeps screening records and training rosters.
  • Screening Committee: three parishioners appointed by the pastor who conduct volunteer interviews and reference checks. Chair: Robert Cheng, screening@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

Frequently asked

My child is in First Communion class. Who has been screened?

Every catechist, assistant and classroom volunteer has completed the full high-risk screening, including a police check and training. You are welcome to ask Sr. Agnes to confirm this for any individual.

I only want to help at the bake sale. Do I need a police check?

No. Low-risk roles need only the application and a short conversation. See the table on the Volunteer Screening page.

What if I am not sure whether what I saw was abuse?

Raise it anyway. Speak to the pastor, the coordinator, or a children's aid society; they will help you think it through. It is always better to ask than to stay silent.

Questions about our Safe Environment practices? Contact Teresa Alvarez at 416-555-0142 ext. 21 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

A third of our parishioners are over 65, and many of them have been here since the church was built. This page gathers everything the parish offers older members — for fun, for prayer, and for the harder seasons of illness and loss.

Prime Time 55+

Coffee and pastries in the hall at 9:15, then something different each week: a speaker (a pharmacist on medications, a lawyer on wills, a police officer on scams), cards and games, chair exercise, a film, or a bus trip — Niagara's shrines in May, the Martyrs' Shrine in June, a Christmas lunch in December. About sixty members; $10 a year. New members are welcomed with a name tag and a seat at a table of people who will remember your name.

Weekly or as wished · Lay Pastoral Visitors

If you cannot come to Mass, a screened visitor brings Holy Communion, the Sunday readings and the bulletin, and stays for a visit. Call the office to arrange.

Anointing & visits

Anointing Masses

February 11 (Our Lady of Lourdes) and October · 11:00 AM, lunch after

A Mass at which anyone who is elderly or unwell may receive the Anointing of the Sick, followed by lunch in the hall.

Rides to Mass

Sunday 9:00 and 11:00 AM · volunteer drivers

Door-to-door rides within the parish for those who no longer drive. Book by Thursday with the office. Wheelchair-accessible taxi vouchers are available for those who need them.

Phone tree & friendly calls

Weekly

A volunteer phones each week to say hello, check in and pass on news. Started in 2020 and never stopped.

Long-term care visits

Weekly · two nearby homes

Communion services and visits at the two long-term-care homes in the parish; monthly Mass at each with Fr. Nguyen.

Bereavement support

Groups and companions

For the loss of a spouse, a friend, a sibling.

Bereavement ministry

Practical support

  • Accessibility: step-free entrance on the east side, elevator to the hall, hearing loop (set your hearing aid to T), large-print missals and bulletins, reserved pews for walkers and wheelchairs. See accessibility.
  • Livestream: the Sunday 11:00 AM and weekday 8:30 AM Masses on YouTube; a volunteer can set up your TV or tablet.

Retired parishioners run the pantry mornings, count the collection, garden, drive, phone, visit, sew, bake and — more than anyone — pray. If you have time now that you did not have at forty, the parish has a place for it. See volunteer, or come to Prime Time on Wednesday and ask.

item.title: Site Guide for Parish Staff
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Who this page is for

The pastor, the parish secretary and whoever looks after the bulletin. No technical background is assumed. Everything described here can be done from a normal web browser.

1. What you are looking at

This demonstration site shows the complete website a parish receives: more than sixty pages covering Mass times, every sacrament, thirty ministries, an events calendar, weekly bulletins, giving, safe environment policies and a contact office. The photographs are free stock images (see the credits); they are swapped for the parish's own photos before launch. The parish name, address, staff and schedule are placeholders that are replaced with yours.

Every page is written with the same building blocks WordPress uses — paragraphs, headings, images, buttons, columns and cards — so nothing has to be rebuilt when the site moves to WordPress. What you see here is what you will get.

65+ pages of finished content
30 ministry pages & directory
1 calendar the office controls
C$48 per year hosting (WordPress.com Personal)

2. Where the site lives

The parish site is hosted on WordPress.com on the Personal plan — about C$4 a month, billed yearly, in the parish's own name. WordPress.com handles security updates, backups and hosting; there is no server for anyone to maintain. Since April 2026 the Personal plan includes everything this design needs:

  • A custom domain (for example stcolumbatoronto.ca), free for the first year, with no advertising on the site.
  • Global Styles, custom fonts and custom CSS — so the colours, typefaces and layouts you see here are reproduced exactly.
  • The Form block (contact, registration, prayer requests), the YouTube block (livestream) and the Google Calendar block (events).
  • 6 GB of storage — enough for years of bulletins and photos.
  • Access to WordPress plugins should the parish ever want more, though this site needs none.

Plan details are published at wordpress.com/pricing and change from time to time; we confirm them with you before the parish signs up.

3. Moving the site onto WordPress.com

This is done once, by us, usually within a week of the parish's go-ahead. You do not need to do anything except approve the content and provide photos.

  1. Create the WordPress.com site and domain

    Registered to the parish's own email address so the parish, not the developer, owns it.

  2. Apply the design

    A standard block theme is installed and its Styles set to the parish palette and fonts; the small custom stylesheet is added under Additional CSS. The header (menu, search, Give button) and footer are built as template parts, so they appear on every page automatically.

  3. Import the pages and photos

    All pages are imported in one step from an export file generated from this demo, with the photos uploaded to the Media Library. Links between pages keep working.

  4. Connect the live pieces

    The parish's YouTube channel is linked to the livestream page, a parish Google Calendar is connected to the events page, and forms are pointed at the office email address.

  5. Review and launch

    The pastor and secretary read every page, we make corrections, and the domain goes live. We then walk the office through the edits below in a one-hour session.

4. Everyday updates the office makes itself

Sign in at yourdomain.ca/wp-admin. Each task below takes a few minutes.

Change Mass or confession times

Pages → Mass Times → Edit. Click the time you want to change, type the new one, and press Update. The home page and footer show the same times; update them in the same way (Appearance → Editor → Footer for the footer). We keep the list of every place a time appears in the parish's handover notes.

Add or change an event

Open the parish Google Calendar (the office already uses it) and add the event with its time, location and a two-sentence description. The calendar on the Events page updates on its own. For a headline event you also want featured on the home page, edit the Home page and change the text in one of the three event cards.

Post this week's bulletin

Pages → Weekly Bulletin → Edit. Click the top entry in the list, duplicate it, change the date and title, then click the PDF button and choose Replace to upload the new PDF from your computer. Press Update. The previous bulletins stay in the archive below.

Add a news item

Pages → Parish News → Edit. Copy the top story block (three dots → Duplicate), change the date, headline, text and photo. To put it on the home page, edit Home and change the first entry in "Parish news".

Update staff, clergy or ministry contacts

Each person is a card on Clergy & Staff; each ministry has its own page with a contact line near the top. Click the text and retype it. To change a photo, click the image → Replace.

Read form submissions

Every contact, registration, prayer request, Mass intention and volunteer form also sends an email to the office address. The full list is under Feedback in the dashboard, where entries can be searched and exported.

Add a completely new page

Pages → Add New. Use the Patterns panel to insert a ready-made layout (card grid, FAQ, people cards, steps) that matches the rest of the site, then add it to the menu under Appearance → Editor → Navigation.

5. Things that stay consistent

The office looks after

  • Mass times, office hours, holiday notices
  • Events in Google Calendar
  • Weekly bulletin PDFs
  • News, photos, ministry contacts
  • Replying to form submissions

We look after (support plan)

  • Design, menus, header and footer
  • Domain and hosting renewals
  • Accessibility and mobile checks
  • New sections or larger changes
  • A yearly review with the pastor

6. Standards this site meets

  • Mobile, tablet and desktop — every page is tested at phone, tablet and laptop widths; the menu becomes a full-screen list on phones and the calendar becomes a list.
  • Accessibility — skip link, keyboard-operable menus, labelled forms, visible focus, alt text on images, colour contrast checked; see the accessibility statement.
  • Search engines — titles and descriptions on every page, structured data for the church and events, a sitemap, and fast-loading resized images.
  • Archdiocese of Toronto — Safe Environment, volunteer screening, misconduct reporting, accessibility and privacy pages are included and linked from every footer.
  • Privacy — forms collect only what the office needs; no advertising trackers.

item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Need help?

Call the confidential line: 416-555-0142, extension 30, and leave a message — a Vincentian calls back within two days. Or come to the pantry on Tuesday or Saturday morning, 10:00 AM to noon, at the hall door on the parking lot. No referral, no paperwork on the first visit, no questions about faith or status.

The Society of St. Vincent de Paul is a lay Catholic organization founded in Paris in 1833 by a 20-year-old student, Frédéric Ozanam, to serve the poor person to person. Our conference of thirty-two members has been at St. Columba since 1958. Last year it served about ninety households a week through the pantry and made 210 home visits.

Food pantry

A week's groceries for the household — rice, pasta, canned fish and vegetables, eggs, milk, fresh produce when we have it, and diapers and formula for families. Tuesdays and Saturdays, 10 AM to noon.

Home visits

Two Vincentians visit, listen, and help with what is actually needed: a rent shortfall, a hydro bill, a bed for a child, a bus pass to a job interview, a referral to a service that can do more.

Seasonal help

Thanksgiving and Christmas hampers (with the Knights), back-to-school supplies in August, winter coats through Coats for Kids, and Christmas gifts for 120 children.

How to give

Food

Bins at every church door, any time. Most needed right now:

  • Rice (2 kg bags), pasta and pasta sauce
  • Canned fish, beans and vegetables
  • Cooking oil, flour, sugar
  • Peanut butter, cereal, oats
  • Baby formula, diapers (sizes 4–6), wipes
  • Toothpaste, soap, feminine hygiene products

Please check dates; we cannot distribute expired food. No glass jars if possible.

Money

Cash goes furthest — the conference buys fresh food wholesale and pays bills directly. Give through the parish giving page designated "St. Vincent de Paul", by envelope marked SSVP, or at the monthly SSVP collection on the last Sunday. Gifts are receipted by the Society. A $50 gift feeds a family for a week; $500 keeps a family in their apartment.

Things

Furniture and clothing go to the Society's stores and depots; call the National Council's Toronto pickup line, which the conference can give you. We cannot store furniture at the parish.

Volunteer

Pantry mornings need sorters, packers and greeters (Tuesday and Saturday, 9:00 AM to 12:30 PM); a monthly commitment is ideal. Home visitors are full members of the conference, attend the meeting on the first Thursday at 7:00 PM, complete high-risk screening and are trained in pairs. Drivers with a car are gold. Students earn service hours on Saturdays. Email ssvp@stcolumbatoronto.ca; president: Rosemary Achebe.

Questions

Do I have to be Catholic, or live in the parish, to get help?

No. The pantry serves anyone in the neighbourhood; home visits are for people living within the parish boundaries, and we refer others to the conference nearest them.

Is my visit confidential?

Absolutely. Vincentians never discuss who they help, and records are kept only as required for the Society's audit.

How often can I come to the pantry?

Once a week. Households register on the second visit (name, address, household size) so that we can plan.

Learn more about the Society at ssvp.ca.

item.title: Vocations
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The word "vocation" simply means "calling." Every baptised person has one: a way of life through which God asks us to love and be loved. Some are called to marriage, some to the priesthood or diaconate, some to religious life, and some to a committed single life of service. None is a consolation prize. St. Columba has given the Church three priests, two permanent deacons and four religious sisters over its seventy years, and hundreds of marriages. We pray for more of all of them.

Priesthood

A diocesan priest serves the people of a particular diocese, usually in parishes, celebrating the sacraments, preaching, teaching and accompanying people through life's biggest moments. Priests for the Archdiocese of Toronto are formed at St. Augustine's Seminary in Scarborough. Formation takes six to eight years after high school or university, and includes philosophy, theology, pastoral placements in parishes, and a year of discernment before entering. A man may also be called to a religious order (Jesuits, Basilians, Franciscans and many others), whose priests live in community and serve according to their order's charism.

Permanent diaconate

Deacons are ordained ministers who proclaim the Gospel, preach, baptise, witness marriages, preside at funerals and lead the Church's works of charity. Most permanent deacons are married men with families and careers; our own Deacon Ferreira spent thirty years as a TTC mechanic. The Archdiocese admits men between 35 and 60, with the consent and involvement of their wives, to a four-year formation program of evening and weekend study. Deacon Ferreira is glad to talk with any man who is curious; reach him at ext. 24.

Consecrated life

Religious sisters, brothers and priests, and consecrated virgins and hermits, give their whole lives to God through vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. Some communities teach, nurse or serve the poor; others are contemplative, devoting their days to prayer. Toronto is home to dozens of communities, from the School Sisters of Notre Dame (Sr. Agnes's community) to the Sisters of Life, the Congregation of St. Basil and the Carmelites. Women and men who feel drawn to religious life usually spend a year or two visiting communities before applying.

Marriage and the single life

Most parishioners are called to marriage, in which a husband and wife become a sign of Christ's faithful love and, God willing, raise a family. Marriage is a true vocation, discerned and prepared for with as much seriousness as ordination; see Marriage and Marriage and Family. Others live a dedicated single life, sometimes by choice and sometimes by circumstance, and pour their freedom into service, work, friendship and the parish. The Church needs them, and their holiness is no less real.

Discernment

How to discern a vocation

Discernment is not a one-time decision but a habit of listening. These steps work for any vocation.

  1. Pray every day

    Ten minutes of quiet with Scripture, and Mass more than once a week if you can. Thursday morning Adoration is a good place to sit with the question.

  2. Talk to someone

    Fr. Moreau, Fr. Nguyen, Deacon Ferreira and Sr. Agnes have all walked this road. An honest conversation is the single most useful step; no one will sign you up for anything.

  3. Get involved

    Serve at the altar, join the choir, help at the food bank. Vocations grow where people are already giving themselves.

  4. Visit

    Attend a discernment evening at the seminary, a "come and see" weekend with a religious community, or an information night for the diaconate. The Office of Vocations lists them all.

  5. Find a spiritual director

    A director meets with you monthly to help you notice where God is moving. Ask our clergy for a referral.

  6. Take the next step

    Apply, get engaged, enter formation. Discernment continues inside the seminary or the novitiate, and marriage preparation is itself discernment.

Office of Vocations, Archdiocese of Toronto

The archdiocesan Office of Vocations runs discernment groups for men and women, retreats, and the annual Vocations Sunday. Its website has profiles of seminarians, a directory of religious communities and a calendar of events: vocationstoronto.ca.

Serra Club

The Serra Club is an international lay association whose members pray and work for vocations. St. Columba parishioners take part in the East Toronto Serra Club, which hosts a dinner for seminarians each Advent, sends birthday cards to every priest and religious from our area, sponsors the "31 Club" (parishioners who commit to attend Mass for vocations on one date each month), and pays for altar-server appreciation outings. Contact: Gerald Okafor, serra@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

A prayer for vocations

Lord Jesus, you called the apostles from their boats and their tables and made them fishers of people. Call from among our families and friends men and women who will serve you as priests, deacons and religious, and give to every one of us the courage to answer the vocation you have prepared for us. Bless our seminarians and novices, sustain our priests and religious, and make our parish a place where callings are heard. Amen.

Prayed at St. Columba on the first Thursday of each month

This prayer is offered after the 8:30 AM Mass on the first Thursday of each month, and the Legion of Mary includes vocations in its weekly intentions. Vocation prayer cards are available at the church entrance.

Frequently asked

How old do you have to be to enter the seminary?

Most men enter between 20 and 35, after at least some university. The Archdiocese also welcomes older candidates with life experience, case by case.

Can a married man become a priest?

In the Latin Church, priests are ordinarily celibate. A married man may be ordained a permanent deacon.

What if I discern and decide it is not for me?

That is a successful discernment. Many men and women spend time in formation and leave with a clearer sense of God's call to marriage or another path, and the Church is grateful for their honesty.

Questions? Speak to any of our clergy after Mass, or contact the parish office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20 to arrange a conversation.

item.title: Volunteer Screening
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for wanting to serve. Before any volunteer begins at St. Columba, we ask them to complete a screening process required by the Archdiocese of Toronto for every parish. It is not a test of your faith or your character; it is a set of ordinary, sensible checks that let parents, seniors and the parish itself trust the people in ministry. Most volunteers finish it in two to three weeks. This page walks through every step so there are no surprises.

Why we screen

Screening is the first line of the Archdiocese's Safe Environment policy. It reduces the chance that someone who would harm a child or vulnerable adult is placed in a position of trust, and it makes sure every volunteer understands the expectations of their role before they start. It also protects you: a clear record that the parish followed its process is your best defence if a complaint is ever made. And it protects the parish's insurance coverage, which depends on the policy being followed.

Low-risk and high-risk ministries

The level of screening depends on the level of trust and access a role involves. The Archdiocese sorts ministries into two categories:

If you are unsure which category your role falls into, the Screening Committee will tell you. When in doubt, the parish treats a role as high-risk.

The steps

  1. Application

    Complete the Volunteer Application Form (available at the office or as a PDF below). It asks for your contact details, the ministry you are interested in, relevant experience, and two references. For high-risk roles it also includes a self-declaration about past offences.

  2. Interview

    A member of the Screening Committee meets with you for 20 to 30 minutes, usually after a weekend Mass or on a weekday evening. It is a friendly conversation about why you want to serve, what the role involves, and any questions you have. For low-risk roles, this may be a phone call.

  3. References

    We contact your two references by phone or email. Choose people who have known you for at least two years and who are not family members; a former employer, teacher, coach or fellow parishioner is ideal.

  4. Police vulnerable-sector check (high-risk only)

    Toronto residents apply online through the Toronto Police Service; residents of other municipalities apply to their local police. The parish gives you a letter confirming you are a volunteer, which waives or reduces the fee in most services. Bring or upload the result to the office; we record that it was received and return the original to you. The check is required before you begin any high-risk role.

  5. Orientation and training

    High-risk volunteers attend the two-hour Safe Environment awareness session, sign the code of conduct, and complete an orientation with their ministry coordinator. Low-risk volunteers receive a short orientation from their coordinator.

  6. Welcome

    Once the file is complete, the coordinator confirms your start date. Your name is added to the ministry roster and you are commissioned with other new volunteers at a Sunday Mass in October.

How long does it take?

Low-risk: usually one to two weeks. High-risk: three to six weeks, mostly waiting for the police check, which the Toronto Police Service currently returns in about two to four weeks online. Start early if you hope to begin in September; applications for fall ministries are best submitted by mid-July.

Renewals

  • High-risk volunteers renew their police check every five years, and sign an annual "offence declaration" in the years between.
  • Safe Environment training is refreshed every three years.
  • All volunteers confirm their contact information and ministry each September.
  • Moving from a low-risk to a high-risk role means completing the additional steps first.

We send reminders two months before a renewal is due. Please do not let a check lapse; a volunteer whose screening is out of date must step back from the ministry until it is renewed.

Your privacy

Screening files are kept in a locked cabinet in the parish office and seen only by the pastor, the Safe Environment Coordinator and the Screening Committee. We record that a police check was received and its date; we do not keep a copy of the check itself. Files are retained for as long as you volunteer and for seven years afterwards, in line with archdiocesan policy. See our Privacy Policy for more.

Frequently asked

I already have a police check from my job or another parish. Can I use it?

If it is a vulnerable-sector check dated within the last twelve months, yes, bring it in. Checks from another Archdiocese of Toronto parish transfer with a phone call between offices.

What if something shows up on my police check?

A record does not automatically exclude you. The pastor and Screening Committee consider the nature of the offence, how long ago it occurred and the role you have applied for, and they will speak with you privately. Some roles will not be possible; others will.

Do teenagers need screening?

Volunteers under 18 complete the application and interview with a parent, and work alongside screened adults. Police checks are not issued to minors.

Is there a fee?

Screening itself is free. If your police service charges for a volunteer check, the parish will reimburse the fee; keep your receipt.

item.title: Volunteer
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Nothing at St. Columba happens without volunteers — not Mass, not the pantry, not the picnic. Volunteering is also the fastest way to stop being a stranger in a big parish: serve beside people for a month and you will have friends. Start small; most roles ask for one or two hours a week or a few Saturdays a year.

Where we need help now

How it works

  1. Tell us what interests you

    Use the form below, or speak to any priest or ministry leader. There is no wrong answer; "I don't know, what do you need?" is a fine start.

  2. A conversation

    The ministry coordinator calls within two weeks to talk about the role, the commitment and your availability, and invites you to see the ministry in action.

  3. Screening

    Every volunteer completes the Archdiocese's screening: a short form and orientation for low-risk roles; for high-risk roles (children, youth, the elderly, money, driving), also an interview, two references and a police vulnerable-sector check, which the parish arranges and pays for. It takes three to six weeks.

  4. Training and start

    Training is specific to the role — from an hour for ushers to a course for catechists. You start alongside an experienced volunteer, and check in with the coordinator after a month.

Volunteer interest form

I'm interested in

Your information is used only to connect you with a ministry. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Thank you. A ministry coordinator will contact you within two weeks.

How volunteers are supported

Every ministry has a coordinator you can call; expenses (mileage, supplies) are reimbursed; training and screening are free; and the parish says thank you properly — at the volunteer appreciation dinner each June, and at the Mass on the feast of St. Columba where volunteers are blessed. Volunteers who wish to step back for a season simply tell their coordinator; nobody is trapped.

I'm under 18.

Altar serving from Grade 3; children's choir from Grade 2; from Grade 9, lectoring, the livestream team, pantry Saturdays and youth leadership — with a parent's consent form. Service hours for school are signed by the coordinator.

I only have a few hours a year.

Then the picnic, the bazaar, the Christmas hampers and the spring garden day are yours. One-off help is real help.

item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The years between leaving home and settling down are when many Catholics drift — not from anger, but because nobody noticed them leave. Our young adult community exists so that does not happen here. About sixty people take part; a dozen of them are on the leadership team with Marcus Lee and Fr. Nguyen.

Sunday 5:00 PM Mass & supper

Weekly · supper in the hall most Sundays, $5

The easiest way in. Sit anywhere; stay for food afterwards. The contemporary ensemble leads the music and needs singers and players.

Theology on Tap

Last Wednesday · 7:30 PM · a nearby pub or the hall

A speaker, a question, a drink, a real conversation. Recent topics: faith and mental health, Catholic social teaching and housing, dating with intention.

Bible study

Thursdays · 7:30 PM · meeting room A (after the parish Bible study)

Small-group lectio on the coming Sunday's Gospel. Forty-five minutes; no homework.

Service

Monthly Saturday

Out of the Cold cooking team in winter, pantry sorting, Habitat builds, refugee family move-ins.

Retreats & pilgrimages

February retreat · summer pilgrimage

A silent weekend in February; in summer a bus to Martyrs' Shrine in Midland or the Oratory in Montreal.

Socials

Every few weeks

Trivia nights, hikes, skating at Nathan Phillips Square, a Christmas party. Newcomers to Toronto especially welcome.

On campus

Students at U of T, TMU, York and the colleges have Catholic chaplaincies of their own — the Newman Centre, campus ministries and residence chaplains — and we work alongside them. Many students worship at St. Columba on Sundays and on campus during the week. See chaplaincies for contacts. If you are in Toronto for a year on exchange or a work placement, you belong here for that year.

Faith, vocation, life

Some of the community are discerning marriage, priesthood or religious life; some are exploring the Church for the first time and join the OCIA group; some are engaged and preparing for marriage; some have just come back after years away and start with confession. Fr. Nguyen offers spiritual direction to young adults on Tuesday evenings by appointment.

Join

Email youngadults@stcolumbatoronto.ca or message Marcus after the 5:00 PM Mass and you will be added to the group chat and the fortnightly email. There is no membership and no fee. Coordinators this year: Priya Nair and Daniel Osei.

I'm older than 35 / younger than 18.

Under 18, see youth ministry. Over 35, everyone is welcome at Theology on Tap and service days; the parish's other groups may also fit.

I don't know anyone.

Nor did anyone else the first week. Tell the person at the supper table you are new; that is what the table is for.

item.title: Youth Ministry
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Being a young Catholic in Toronto is not easy, and it is not meant to be done alone. Youth ministry at St. Columba is led by Marcus Lee, a full-time youth and young adult minister, with a team of twelve screened adult and young-adult leaders. About 110 young people take part each year.

Grades 6 to 8

EDGE

1st and 3rd Fridays · 7:00 – 9:00 PM · youth room and hall. Middle school is the age of big questions and small confidence. EDGE nights mix games, snacks, a short talk on the theme of the month, small groups led by high-school and adult leaders, and ten minutes of prayer. Parents drop off at 6:50 and pick up at 9:00 sharp.

Register for EDGE

Grades 9 to 12

LIFE TEEN

2nd and 4th Fridays · 7:00 – 9:30 PM. Life Nights alternate between catechesis ("issue nights" on faith, relationships, mental health, vocation), social nights and service nights, and once a month end in adoration with praise and worship. Teens are welcome to bring friends of any faith. Leadership roles — worship team, small-group leader, tech — are open from Grade 11.

Register for LIFE TEEN

More than Fridays

Sunday 5:00 PM Mass

Every Sunday · supper in the hall after, most weeks

The youth and young adult Mass with the contemporary ensemble; teens serve, read and sing.

Retreats

August (LIFE TEEN) · March (EDGE)

A weekend away with Mass, adoration, canoes and no phones. Subsidized; nobody stays home for money.

Summer camp

Two weeks in July · ages 6–12 · teen counsellors

A day camp run by our high-schoolers — the best leadership training we have.

Service hours

Ongoing · pantry, picnic, Out of the Cold, camp

Signed hours for high-school community service and for Confirmation.

Confirmation

Grade 7 · monthly Sundays

The youth team leads the Confirmation retreat and sessions with Sr. Agnes.

Confirmation

Praise & worship nights

Monthly · see the calendar

Music, adoration, confession and pizza; open to all ages 12 and up.

Calendar

Safe environment

Every adult leader has completed the Archdiocese of Toronto's volunteer screening, including a police vulnerable-sector check and Safe Environment training, and two screened adults are present at every activity. Parents receive a permission form for every off-site event, and photos are only shared with written consent. Concerns of any kind may be brought to Marcus, to Fr. Moreau, or directly to the Archdiocese — see Safe Environment.

For parents

How do I register, and what does it cost?

Registration is online (or on paper at the office) each September and stays open all year; a $40 annual fee covers snacks and materials and is waived on request. Retreats and camp are priced separately with bursaries available.

My teen is not sure about faith.

Perfect. Youth ministry is for teenagers who are figuring it out, and honest doubt is welcome. Many of our most committed leaders started as reluctant Grade 9s brought by a friend.

We don't go to St. Columba's school or even this parish.

Any young person is welcome regardless of school or parish; about a third of our teens come from outside the parish boundaries.

How do I stay informed?

A parent email goes out every second week; teens are on a moderated group chat run by two leaders. Follow the parish on Instagram for photos and reminders.

Marcus Lee, Youth & Young Adult Minister — ext. 27, youth@stcolumbatoronto.ca.
